levels.title: The interview as an instrument: elicitation, observation, translation and honest documents

lessons.title: The architecture of a psychiatric assessment interview: what each phase is for
lessons.explanation:
Psychiatry has few physical instruments. Its primary measuring device is a conversation, and like any instrument it has a design, a range and failure modes. This lesson maps the design. Everything here is education about how clinicians reason and talk. It is not a method for diagnosing anyone, and it contains no treatment advice.

A psychiatric interview is usually described as if it were a form being read aloud: demographic details, presenting complaint, past psychiatric history, medical history, family history, personal history, drug and alcohol history, forensic history, risk, mental state. That list is a memory aid, not an order of operations. Practically, the interview has four functional phases, and each buys something the others cannot.

The opening phase establishes the frame: who you are, what you already know, how long you have, what happens to what is said, what the person can refuse, and what they want out of the encounter. Its product is consent and orientation, and its failure mode is a person who does not know why they are talking.

The narrative phase is the one most often skipped. The clinician asks an open question and then gets out of the way: tell me what has brought you here, in your own words, starting wherever makes sense. Its product is the person's own account, with their own emphasis, in their own sequence. Its failure mode is a clinician who interrupts after ninety seconds because they recognise a familiar pattern. Julie Nordgaard and colleagues make a claim about this phase that is worth memorising in its stark form: they write that patients' abilities of self-description vary, that some dissimulate by hiding experiences they consider strange or shameful, and that one sometimes obtains the information one is looking for only by asking about something else, or by not asking at all [1]. That sentence is an argument for a long narrative phase and for patience in later ones.

The focused phase is where the clinician takes responsibility. Having heard the account, the clinician now covers ground the person did not spontaneously raise: sleep, appetite, energy, enjoyment, concentration, anxiety, panic, obsessions, compulsions, trauma, mood elevation, unusual experiences, cognition, and so on, down whatever list the service uses. Its product is coverage. Its failure mode is turning coverage into an interrogation in which the clinician's list crowds out the person's meaning. A useful marker: if the whole interview could have been conducted with a template and a stranger, coverage won without a narrative.

The closing phase is the most neglected and the most useful. The clinician summarises what they have understood, in plain language, and offers the person the chance to correct it. Its products are three: the corrections themselves, which are frequent; the person's sense of being met rather than processed; and a shared record of what has been agreed. Its failure mode is a summary that is really a verdict, delivered as news.

Running alongside all four phases is a second activity, the observation pass. Throughout, the clinician is also attending to what can be seen and heard: appearance, grooming, behaviour in the room, speech rate and volume, emotional expression, how the person responds to being disagreed with, whether they look at their watch or at the door. This is not a phase, which is a common confusion; it is a parallel channel, and lesson 63 is devoted to keeping it separate from what the person reports.

Two structural traps are worth naming here. The first is to treat a very structured instrument as a substitute for the interview. Nordgaard, Sass and Parnas describe the fully structured interview as a set of pre-specified questions in fixed sequence with responses rated positive, negative or threshold, and they argue it rests on assumptions: that symptoms are discrete, thing-like, context-free objects rather than meaningful experiences, and that a fixed order yields valid information about an experience that may be hard to put into words at all [1]. They conclude, in their words, that the fully structured interview is "neither theoretically adequate nor practically valid in obtaining psycho-diagnostic information" [1]. That conclusion is contested, and it should be presented as a position rather than as settled fact: structured instruments exist because unstructured interviews proved unreliable between clinicians, and reliability across raters is a real achievement. The honest statement is that structure buys repeatability and can cost validity, that the trade-off is different in research and in a first clinical meeting, and that a clinician who has never interviewed without a template has no way to notice what the template is filtering out.

The second trap is phase inflation. A first assessment of ninety minutes cannot contain four phases done properly if two of them are consumed by paperwork. Something has to be deferred, and the discipline is to decide consciously what is deferred and to say so in the note, rather than to discover afterwards that the narrative phase never happened.
lessons.example:
Consider a fictional 34-year-old woman referred by her general practitioner with three months of poor sleep and low mood, who arrives with a completed symptom questionnaire scoring in the moderately severe range. Two clinicians interview her.

The first clinician begins with the questionnaire. She reads each item, the patient answers, and the encounter produces a tidy severity score, a diagnosis-shaped summary and a plan. The questionnaire is administered correctly and the notes are clean. Now look at what was foreclosed. The patient's own account was never elicited, so nobody learns that her sleep changed in the same week her brother moved out of the country, that she has been sleeping in the afternoon because nights are when the intrusive images from an earlier assault return, and that she has told nobody about the images because a previous clinician told her they were a long time ago. The questionnaire asked about sleep, mood, appetite, concentration and guilt. It did not ask what changed, in what order, or in what context, because it was not designed to.

The second clinician covers the same questionnaire items, and does so last. Twenty-five minutes go to the narrative: the patient is invited to say what has happened, and is not interrupted except for the smallest encouragers. The clinician takes notes in the patient's own words and marks, in a separate column, observations made during the telling. The narrative surfaces the brother's departure, the afternoon sleeping, the images, and the previous dismissal. The clinician now runs the focused pass with different questions than would otherwise have been asked, some about things the patient raised and some about areas she never mentioned, and only then administers the questionnaire. The score comes out the same, moderately severe. The formulation that follows is completely different from the first clinician's, because the same score can sit on top of a bereavement-related sleep collapse, a trauma-driven night-time avoidance pattern, or both.

Notice the cost of the second approach. It took longer, it produced more uncertainty, and it made the note messier, because the clinician has to record what the patient said and what they noticed and what they think, in three different voices. Notice also what the first approach did not lose: it produced a number, and numbers track change over time. The argument is not that questionnaires are bad. It is that the sequence determines what the subsequent reasoning can be made of: a narrative first, coverage second, instruments third, summary last.
lessons.question: A trainee says the interview should move straight to the focused list of symptoms, because the narrative phase mostly produces irrelevant detail. What is the strongest reply?
lessons.answer: The narrative phase is the only part of the interview that reveals what the person considers relevant, and later focused questions are chosen on the basis of it, so cutting it short removes the information used to decide what to ask next.
lessons.distractor: The narrative phase is required because guidelines forbid asking direct questions about symptoms until the person has described them spontaneously, so a direct question asked first is invalid.
lessons.correction: Guidelines do not forbid direct questioning; NICE's case-identification questions for depression are themselves direct, closed questions used at the start of a pathway. The argument for narrative first is about information, not permission: it is where context, sequence and the person's own priorities appear, and Nordgaard and colleagues also note that people who conceal shameful experiences may only give the information when it is not asked for directly, which is an argument for breadth before depth. A service may legitimately reverse the order in a crisis, and a trainee should be able to say what that reordering costs.

depth.definitions: The history is the account of what has happened and is happening, assembled from the person and from other sources. The mental status examination (MSE) is the structured description of the person's state during the encounter, organised into categories such as appearance, behaviour, speech, mood, affect, thought process, thought content, perception, cognition, insight and judgement [2]. A symptom is something the person experiences and reports; a sign is something the clinician observes. A structured interview fixes the questions and their sequence; a semi-structured interview fixes the domains to be covered but leaves the wording and order conversational; an unstructured interview fixes neither [1]. The observation pass is the continuous parallel activity of noticing what can be seen and heard. Declared provenance is the practice of marking each statement in a note as reported, observed, measured or inferred, which is taught in lesson 63 and applied in lesson 70.
depth.mechanism: Why does sequence matter so much? Three reasons, each with a limit. First, elicitation: open questions produce longer and more detailed accounts, which is why the SAMHSA motivational interviewing advisory tells providers to use open questions to invite people to tell their story and to understand their goals, values and beliefs [3]. The limit is that open questions are inefficient when a specific fact is required, and they depend on the person being able to narrate. Second, recall architecture: people recall in blocks and by association, so a fixed sequence can leave a memory unretrieved because the cue that would have opened it was never used. This is why Nordgaard and colleagues' remark that information sometimes arrives only when it is not requested directly is coherent with ordinary memory research rather than mysterious [1]. Third, and least discussed, opportunity cost: every minute spent on a template item is a minute not spent on what this specific person is trying to say, and the two costs are not symmetric, because the template item can be covered later and the person's willingness to narrate may not return. The mechanism also has a documented limit. Structured interviews were introduced precisely because unstructured interviewing was unreliable, and the fact that a fixed order can miss meaning does not establish that a conversational order is more accurate; it establishes that reliability and validity are different properties, which lesson 65 takes up with the actual agreement data.
depth.secondExample: Now run the phase map through a crisis interview rather than an outpatient one. A fictional 58-year-old man is brought to an emergency department at two in the morning by police after shouting in the street. The four-phase design does not survive contact with this setting in its outpatient form, and pretending otherwise is a failure of skill rather than fidelity. Consent and orientation still come first, but compressed to a sentence, and repeated later when he is more able to take it in. The narrative phase is still attempted, because a person's own account of how he came to be in the street at two in the morning is the single most informative thing available, but it may have to wait until immediate medical needs are addressed. The focused phase is reordered: physical causes of an acute change in behaviour come before any psychological interpretation, which is the ordering that lesson 54 sets out in detail, and immediate safety and basic needs come before history that can be obtained tomorrow. Coverage is explicitly deferred and the note says so, with a time for the fuller assessment. The closing phase changes shape too: it becomes a short, repeated explanation of what is happening next, because the person may not be in a state to correct a summary but is entitled to know where they are going. The lesson transfers: the phases are functions to be discharged, not a fixed script, and when a phase is deferred the writing must record the deferral.
depth.mistake: The commonest error is to confuse the interview form with the interview. A trainee who has learned that assessment 'covers' twenty headings may believe that an encounter in which all twenty were ticked is complete, when nothing was elicited that was not already on the form. The diagnostic correction is to look at the note and ask which sentences could only have been written by someone who had listened to this particular person. If the answer is none, coverage happened and assessment did not. A second error runs the other way: treating the narrative as sacred and refusing to direct the interview at all, which in practice means a person in distress is left to organise the conversation unaided, and a clinician who never asks about cognition, substance use or safety will miss what nobody volunteers. A third error is to treat the MSE as a separate appointment. It is not a second event; it is a description of this event, and the material for it accrues from the first hello, which is why a clinician who starts taking notes about behaviour only after the history is finished has thrown most of the data away. A fourth error, subtler, is writing the summary as a conclusion. The closing phase exists to be corrected; a summary delivered as a decision cannot be.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Choose a fictional setting for one assessment interview and one fictional person, then produce a phase map with timings for a 45-minute encounter: opening, narrative, focused, closing, and the observation pass noted as continuous. Under each phase write one sentence stating its intended product and one sentence stating what you deliberately defer and why. Then write a 120-word note about the fictional person that separates reported, observed and inferred material, and finally answer this question in one paragraph: what in your map would you change if the person arrived unable to speak your language, and what would you change if they arrived with a written list of questions they wanted answered? Model response and self-review rubric: a strong phase map gives the narrative phase at least a quarter of the time and names a specific deferral rather than 'more detail later'. A strong note marks provenance sentence by sentence. A weak map allocates time to headings, leaves no deferral, and answers the language question by planning to use a family member, which lesson 64 explains is a documented source of distortion. A weak note contains at least one sentence in which an inference is written in the grammar of an observation, such as 'patient was guarded and minimising', where neither guardedness nor minimisation is anything the clinician could have observed directly.
depth.summary: An interview is an instrument with four functional phases, an observation pass that runs continuously, and a set of costs attached to how time is allocated. The opening buys consent and orientation; the narrative buys the person's own account and the cues that direct everything after it; the focused pass buys coverage of what was not volunteered; the closing buys correction and shared understanding. Structure is a trade-off: fixing questions and their order improves agreement between clinicians and can suppress meaning, which is why the strongest position is not 'structured versus unstructured' but 'what is this instrument for, and what is it filtering out'. The observation pass is not a phase. Where a phase is deferred, the note must say so, because a deferred phase and a neglected one look identical on paper unless the writer distinguishes them.

visual.title: Phase map of a 45-minute assessment interview with a continuous observation channel
visual.description: A horizontal timeline in four labelled blocks - opening, narrative, focused coverage, closing summary - with a single bar spanning the whole timeline beneath them marked 'observation pass: appearance, behaviour, speech, affect, response to disagreement'. Deferred items are shown as a separate column at the right, each with the time or setting in which it will be covered.
steps: Block 1, opening (about 4 minutes): frame, consent, what the person wants from the encounter; product is orientation, not information.
Block 2, narrative (about 12 minutes): one open invitation, then minimal encouragers; product is the person's own account, sequence and emphasis.
Block 3, focused coverage (about 22 minutes): domains the person did not raise, chosen in the light of the narrative; product is coverage, not interrogation.
Block 4, closing summary (about 7 minutes): read back what was understood and invite correction; product is correction and a shared record.
Continuous bar: observation recorded in a column separate from reported speech, so the two channels can be told apart later.
Right-hand column: deferred items, each with the time or route by which it will be covered, so a deferral is visible and not mistaken for an omission.

lessons.title: Question form and silence: open, closed, funnel, and the deliberate pause
lessons.explanation:
Two tools do most of the work in an assessment interview: the shape of the question and the management of pauses. Both are teachable, both have evidence behind them, and both are routinely used badly in opposite directions - constant closed questioning on one side, a veneration of silence on the other. This lesson is education about interviewing technique. It contains no diagnostic criteria and no treatment instructions, and it is not a script for interrogating anyone.

Start with question form. An open question invites a narrative and does not specify what information is wanted: what has been happening, tell me about the last few weeks, what was that like. A directive question narrows to a domain but still invites an account: what is your sleep been like? A closed question specifies the answer space: are you sleeping less than four hours a night? A leading question embeds the answer: you must be exhausted, aren't you? In a well-run interview these forms are not competitors; they are sequenced, which is the funnel: open, then directive, then closed, then a check.

The reason the sequence runs in that direction is not politeness. It is evidential. The SAMHSA advisory on motivational interviewing, drawing on Miller and Rollnick, tells providers to use open questions to invite clients to tell their story and to obtain a meaningful understanding of their goals, values and beliefs, and it notes that skilled practitioners offer reflections more often than they ask questions [1]. The advisory also defines the four interwoven processes of the approach - partnership, acceptance, compassion and evocation - in which the provider influences gently but the person drives the conversation [1]. Whatever the treatment context, the interviewing implication transfers: an open question produces material whose relevance the speaker chose, which is why it can reveal things no list contains.

Closed questions have two specific virtues and one specific vice. The virtues are precision and comparability: they pin down a fact that a narrative may circle, and they can be counted across occasions. The vice is that a closed question about a feeling invites a yes: response styles vary between people, but the general tendency to agree with a well-formed proposition when a question is put by a clinician is documented well enough that a bare yes to a leading question should not be treated as a finding. The practical repair is the check: after any closed question used to establish something important, ask for the evidence in the person's terms, which usually means returning to an open or directive form and listening to what comes.

Now silence. Silence in an interview is not one thing, and the research literature about it is mostly about psychotherapy rather than psychiatric assessment, which is the first limit on how much can be claimed. A conversation-analytic study of silence in psychodynamic therapy distinguishes three ways silence behaves: it can retroactively close a topic; it can be shaped as an intra-topic silence that extends the emotional content of what is being discussed; and it can itself become a relevant activity, so that the absence of talk is treated as disruptive to the ongoing work [2]. The same study notes that in the intra-topic case, silence leads to an extension of the implicit emotional content of the topic, which the therapist's interventions then enhance [2]. A 2024 systematic literature review of pauses of silence in psychotherapy, following PRISMA guidance, sets out to describe the meaning and functions of pauses in the process rather than to test an outcome [3]. So the honest reading of the evidence is: silence has describable functions that depend on context, and there is no good basis for the claim that longer silences are therapeutically superior, or that a clinician should tolerate any duration of silence as a matter of principle.

What the two literatures together do support is a small set of practical judgements. Silence after a person has just said something difficult is usually doing something: it holds the space open rather than closing the exchange. Silence used as an instrument in the middle of a person's account to extract more, particularly in a setting where the clinician holds the power, can be experienced as pressure or as withholding, and the same technique lands differently with different people. Silence when the person is acutely distressed, disorganised or unable to monitor the interaction is not a technique at all; it is a gap that will be filled with whatever the person's state supplies. And silence after a question that was too vague to answer is a signal that the question failed, not that the person is withholding.
lessons.example:
Below is one fictional exchange written three times. The patient is a 26-year-old man attending a first appointment, and the clinical interest is in unusual experiences that he has mentioned only obliquely.

Version one, closed and leading. Clinician: 'Do you hear voices?' Patient: 'No.' Clinician: 'So you don't hear voices. And no one is talking about you, no one is watching you?' Patient: 'No.' Clinician: 'And you would tell me if you were, wouldn't you?' Patient: 'Yes.' Four questions, four answers, all of them correct as utterances, and nothing has been established. The clinician has confirmed a headcount of two symptom words and has no idea whether the patient understood 'voices' to mean the same thing they do.

Version two, closed but not leading, with a check. Clinician: 'Have you noticed any experiences that other people wouldn't understand or that you've kept to yourself?' Patient: 'Not really.' Clinician: 'I ask because people describe all sorts of things here - sounds that aren't there, a sense that things aren't quite right with the world, feeling that you're being watched. Does any of that sound familiar, even slightly?' Patient: 'Not watched. But I get this feeling that things are being arranged for me. Like the radio is doing it on purpose.' The check produced the specific term the patient will use, which is now available for every later question and which no single closed item would have elicited.

Version three, open with a deliberate pause. Clinician: 'You said earlier that things have felt strange for a while. Tell me about the strangest of those moments.' Patient: 'In the shop, in March.' Then, silence, held for about fifteen seconds, with no comment from the clinician. Patient: 'It was the feeling that the whole aisle was arranged. That I was supposed to be there. Like something was showing me something.' The pause is not extraction; it is the space in which the person decides whether to say the next part, and it is what makes this version longer and stranger-sounding than the others.

Now compare the yields. Version one produced two noes and a compliance check. Version two produced a specific experience and the language the person uses for it, because the closed question was followed by a check that traded precision for disclosure. Version three produced the same specific experience embedded in the person's own account of when it started, which is exactly the material a clinician needs in order to decide what to ask next. Note two costs of version three: it took longer, and it required the clinician to tolerate the discomfort of not knowing what was coming. Note also its risk, which is real: with a person who is acutely distressed or disorganised, fifteen seconds of silence may be fifteen seconds of unmonitored distress, and a clinician who treats the pause as a rule rather than a tool will eventually use it on someone it hurts.
lessons.question: A clinician wants to establish whether a person has been sleeping badly, in about the same time as a single closed question would take. What is the better approach?
lessons.answer: Ask one directive question that invites a description of recent nights, and follow only if needed with a closed question to pin the pattern down, so the account is the person's and the specific fact is still fixed.
lessons.distractor: Ask the closed question first and then ask the same question again in open form, because repeating what has already been asked in a different form is what the interviewing literature calls a check.
lessons.correction: A check is not a repetition of the same content in a different grammatical form; it is an invitation to the person to supply their own grounds for the answer, which means going back to description and then moving to specifics only for what matters. Repeating a question in two forms invites a person to think they answered wrongly, which is why the interviewing literature treats repetition as one of the roadblocks to listening rather than a technique. Also note what the exercise trades: the directive version is slightly less comparable across occasions, and if the clinician needs a count for follow-up then a closed item is the correct instrument and should be used deliberately, with its limits recorded.

depth.definitions: An open question invites a free account and does not specify the information required; a directive question names a domain but still invites an account; a closed question offers a restricted answer space; a leading question supplies the expected answer inside the question. An invitation is a prompt for more narrative on material the person has already mentioned. The funnel is a deliberate sequence from open to directive to closed. Reflective listening is the practice of offering back what the person seems to mean, in their terms, so that they can confirm or correct it [1]. Silence can be classified by its interactional work: topic-closing, intra-topic, or treated by the participants as an activity in its own right [2]. Response style is a person's tendency to agree or disagree with propositions put to them, which is a property of the interaction rather than a finding about the person. None of these terms is a diagnostic category.
depth.mechanism: Why does question form change what comes back? Three mechanisms, in order of evidential strength. First, information specification: a closed question defines the answer space, so the person's reply is confined to it, whereas an open question leaves the person to decide what is relevant, which is why narrative phases surface material that no item list contains [1]. Second, conversation structure: in ordinary talk, a question sets up an expectation of a particular kind of answer, and a person who is being assessed is usually orienting to the clinician's expectations rather than to their own recall. Third, and weakest, is the suggestion effect: a leading question can shape what a person reports, and while the mechanism is debated, the practical consequence is uncontroversial, which is that an answer to a leading question is weak evidence. The mechanism for silence is different and less well evidenced. The conversation-analytic account is that silence acquires its meaning retroactively, from what the participants do next: if the therapist's next turn summarises, the silence is reading as closing the topic; if the therapist lets the silence stand and the patient extends the emotional content, it reads as intra-topic [2]. That is an argument about how meaning is made in sequence, not a claim that silence produces therapeutic benefit, and the systematic review of pauses frames its work as description of functions rather than evaluation of effects [3]. The transferable point is that a pause is not a technique with a fixed effect; it is an event whose effect is supplied by context, the person's state, and what the clinician does next.
depth.secondExample: Consider the same technique applied to a fictional 44-year-old woman who has been referred after a period of heavy drinking and who arrives openly angry about the referral, having been told by her employer that she must attend. The funnel logic inverts here, and the reason is worth understanding rather than memorising. In a first appointment with a person who did not choose to attend, an open question about what has been happening is very likely to produce a speech about the referral rather than about the drinking, and a clinician who then sits in silence is likely to be experienced as either judging or waiting to pounce. The motivational interviewing advisory's answer is structural rather than verbal: partnership and acceptance are two of its four processes, the provider influences gently and the person drives the conversation, and practitioners offer reflections more often than questions [1]. Concretely, the clinician spends the first phase on what the person wants from an encounter they did not ask for, uses closed questions to establish practical facts efficiently and without drama, and uses reflection instead of silence to keep the exchange open. The general rule this case teaches is that silence and open questioning are tools whose value depends on who asked for the meeting and why; the person who chose to be there can be given room, and the person who was sent is first owed a reason to talk.
depth.mistake: The single most common error is treating a bare denial as a negative finding. A person asked 'do you hear voices?' who says 'no' has told the clinician that, in their understanding of 'voices', they do not have that experience now, and nothing more. The interview literature examined in lesson 61 is a useful corrective: a significant number of patients dissimulate, typically by hiding aspects of psychopathology they consider shameful or strange, so a bare negative more often means 'not as I understand the word' than 'nothing of the kind is there'. The remedy for a negative answer is a follow-up question about the experience rather than about the word, which is the difference between a checklist and an examination. A second error is the mirror image: treating every pause as productive. The silence literature describes functions, and the same pause that holds a space open for one person is experienced as pressure by another and as abandonment by a third; a clinician who has adopted silence as a style rather than a choice has given up the ability to tell which is happening. A third error is asking the same question twice in different grammatical forms and calling it a check, which teaches the person that their first answer was wrong. A fourth is asking about several things at once, which reliably produces an answer to whichever part the person found easiest. And a fifth, which is the quietest, is using an open question in a way that is really a closed question in disguise: 'tell me about how depressed you have been' is not open, it is a proposition with the answer built in, and people are generally too polite to say so.
depth.application: Non-blocking task, in two parts. Part one: take these four questions and rewrite each in one open form and one directive form, then state which of the three you would use first with a person who has just arrived and why. The four are: 'do you drink alcohol?' 'are you sleeping?' 'you're not hearing anything unusual, are you?' 'how bad is the low mood out of ten today?' Part two: write eight consecutive lines of a fictional interview about a topic of your choosing, and beside each line label the question form and mark where a pause occurred and what work it did. Model response and self-review rubric: a strong rewrite of 'do you drink alcohol?' is not 'tell me about your drinking' but something like 'what part does alcohol play in your week?', which asks about function rather than quantity and contains no verdict. A strong piece of dialogue shows at least one closed question followed by a check, at least one leading question identified as leading and repaired, and at least one pause placed after a difficult statement rather than in the middle of a factual answer. A weak submission rewrites everything into open questions and reads as an interrogation in the opposite direction, with no precision anywhere, and no silence at all. If your dialogue contains a question with two objects, or a question that states the answer, mark it and rewrite it: those are the two forms most likely to produce data you will later mistake for a finding.
depth.summary: Question form and silence are the two levers of elicitation, and both work by controlling how much of the answer the person is allowed to choose. Open questions hand the choice to the person and produce accounts whose relevance the clinician could not have predicted; directive questions narrow the domain while keeping the account; closed questions specify the answer and buy precision and comparability at the cost of breadth and of a vulnerability to agreement; leading questions manufacture answers and should be recognised on sight. The funnel sequences these forms deliberately rather than mixing them at random. Silence is a context-dependent event rather than a technique: the psychotherapy literature describes its functions, most of it is observational and none of it licenses the claim that more silence is better, and its meaning is supplied by what the clinician does next and by the person's state. The transfer to any new setting is a single question: for this person, in this phase, with this power imbalance, what does the person get to decide?

visual.title: The funnel: question forms in sequence, with pauses marked
visual.description: Four nested boxes narrowing from left to right, labelled open, directive, closed, check, with example wordings inside each. Above the boxes a row of small markers shows where a pause belongs (after a difficult statement, after a vague question is answered thinly) and where it does not (in the middle of a factual answer, with a person who is acutely distressed).
steps: Box 1 - open: 'what has been happening?' Invites a free account; the person chooses what is relevant.
Box 2 - directive: 'what has your sleep been like?' Names a domain, still invites description.
Box 3 - closed: 'are you sleeping less than four hours?' Specifies the answer space; precise and comparable, and vulnerable to agreement.
Box 4 - check: 'what makes you say that?' Returns the grounds for the answer to the person, so the specific fact rests on their account rather than on a yes.
Marker above: pause placed after a difficult statement held for a short interval, then the person continues or does not, and the clinician follows their lead.
Marker below: pause avoided with a person who is acutely distressed or disorganised, where the gap would be filled by their state rather than by reflection.

lessons.title: Reported and observed: keeping two channels of data apart
lessons.explanation:
An assessment produces two kinds of material, and almost every serious error in psychiatric writing begins with confusing them. One channel is what the person reports: their pain, their sleep, their beliefs, their account of last Tuesday. The other is what the clinician observes: how the person looks, speaks, sits, and responds. This lesson is about the discipline of keeping them apart in reasoning and in writing. It is education about assessment method, not diagnosis or treatment, and no instrument or instruction here should be applied to anyone.

The two channels are not equally reliable, and they are not unreliable in the same direction. Reported data has the advantage of access: only the person can tell you what a hallucination is like, what the voices say, or what the shape of a depressive day feels like from inside. It has the disadvantage of being produced for a purpose. A person may minimise to avoid a hospital admission, exaggerate to obtain help, misremember, or simply have no words for an experience that is not part of ordinary vocabulary. Nordgaard and colleagues observe that some patients dissimulate by hiding experiences they consider strange or shameful, and that a diagnosis resting on a symptom list is vulnerable to exactly this [1]. Observed data has the opposite profile: it does not depend on the person's cooperation, but it depends entirely on the clinician's interpretation, and interpretations are where stereotypes, cultural expectations and first impressions do their work.

The mental status examination is the field's canonical answer to this problem, and its internal division is instructive. StatPearls defines mood as the person's subjective description of their feelings in their own words, determined by asking the person directly and documented with quotations transcribing the response verbatim; affect by contrast is described as the clinician's interpretation of the person's observed expression through non-verbal language, with terms such as euthymic, blunted, labile or incongruent [2]. Those two sentences contain the whole distinction: one category is recorded in the person's voice, the other in the clinician's, and the two are never to be merged into a single word like 'depressed'. The same source goes further and states the operational rule that matters most: observing behaviour requires objective evaluation with subjective history from the person, and if the subjective and objective do not align, the clinician needs to remain neutral [2]. Neutrality here does not mean indifference. It means the note records the divergence and stops there, because the divergence is the finding.

There is a third kind of material that must not be smuggled into either channel: inference. 'Appears to be minimising', 'seems frightened of her partner', 'is clearly not taking the medication' are all conclusions. They may be right. They are not observations, and writing them in the grammar of observations is how a guess becomes a fact that the next clinician inherits. The workable pattern is a three-part note: reported (the person's words), observed (what was seen and heard, with the concrete detail that supports it), inferred (a marked judgement with a stated basis, or an explicit statement that no basis is available yet).

The reason this matters is not pedantry. The replication study examined in lesson 65 lists over-reliance on self-report as a proposed reason for misdiagnosis with a structured instrument, alongside vulnerability to response set in people who are dissimulating and a strong diagnosis-and-comorbidity focus [3]. The same authors report that in an earlier first-admission sample, some patients denied all their psychotic symptoms and a third revealed only some, so a system that takes report at face value and never asks what the clinician has seen will systematically miss cases. But the reverse failure is equally documented in ordinary practice: a person whose reported distress is not visible in their behaviour is described as not really suffering, and observed composure is allowed to outvote a clear statement of despair. The evidence does not license either move, and the reason is structural. Reported and observed data are measurements of different things, so one does not correct the other.
lessons.example:
Here is the same fictional encounter written twice. The person is a 52-year-old man attending a follow-up appointment after a period of treatment he has told his sister he intends to stop.

First version, blended. 'Mr A continues to deny any difficulties. He remains guarded and minimising, and his affect is shallow, suggesting he is not engaged with treatment. He reports no side effects. Insight remains poor.' Read carefully and almost nothing survives. 'Denies any difficulties' is report, and it is probably accurate as a paraphrase of the words used. 'Guarded and minimising' is an inference about his motives presented as a manner of speaking. 'Affect shallow' is the clinician's interpretation, which is legitimate as an observation, but with no concrete detail attached, it is unfalsifiable. 'Suggesting he is not engaged' is inference built on inference. 'No side effects' is report. 'Insight poor' is a global judgement with no content about what he said, which lesson 67 takes apart in detail. The note is unreadable by anyone else: a clinician receiving this person would not know what he actually said, what was actually seen, or where the writer stopped knowing.

Second version, separated. 'Reported: sleep 6 hours a night, waking once; appetite normal; no headache or nausea; says "the tablets are doing nothing for me and I want to stop them". Says mood is "fine now". Observed: arrived 10 minutes early, was polite and cooperative, maintained eye contact, speech normal in rate and volume; when the question about stopping was asked he looked at the floor and answered in a single sentence with a shrug, then changed the subject to his daughter's exam results; no tearfulness seen during 30 minutes. Inferred: his report of improvement is not accompanied by behaviour consistent with settled mood, and the topic change when treatment was mentioned may be avoidance or may be ordinary diffidence; unclear which, and I have not yet asked what stopping would mean to him. Unknown: anything about the last two weeks between appointments other than what he says; no collateral information obtained.'

The second note takes three times as long and contains no conclusion at all. It is far more useful. It tells the next clinician exactly where the doubt is: is the change of subject avoidance? It records the single most important thing the person said, in his words, including the request to stop. It notices something easy to miss, that he arrived early, which is a behaviour and might bear on how he feels about the appointments. And it names its own ignorance rather than papering over it. Note also what it deliberately does not do: it does not resolve the divergence between report and behaviour by declaring one of them true. That resolution is not available from a 30-minute meeting, and claiming it would be the error.
lessons.question: A person says their mood is fine, but during the appointment they cry twice while describing their week. How should this be documented?
lessons.answer: Record both, each in its own channel and in its own detail: what the person said about their mood, and what was observed and when, with the divergence left explicit and no resolution invented.
lessons.distractor: Record the observed crying as the more objective finding, since behaviour cannot be faked, and note that the person's reported mood is unreliable.
lessons.correction: The claim that behaviour cannot be faked is false as a general statement, and it is beside the point: reported and observed data measure different things, which is precisely why the mental status examination keeps mood and affect as separate categories with mood quoted verbatim and affect described as the clinician's interpretation. NICE also treats the person's own account of symptoms as a primary source when language or communication difficulties are present. The temptation to privilege observation is strongest when observation matches what the clinician expected, which is the definition of the bias the separation exists to catch.

depth.definitions: Reported data is anything the person states about their experience, history or circumstances, including their own explanations. Observed data is what the clinician perceives with their senses during the encounter: appearance, behaviour, speech, movement, emotional expression, responsiveness. Inferred data is a conclusion drawn from one or both, such as disengagement, avoidance or deliberate concealment. Mood is the person's subjective description of feeling in their own words, recorded verbatim [2]; affect is the clinician's interpretation of observed expression, with descriptors such as euthymic, blunted, labile or incongruent [2]. Congruence and incongruence describe the fit between mood and affect, and the descriptors are descriptions of the fit rather than findings about its cause [2]. Divergence is the honest label for a mismatch that has not been explained. Provenance is the marker attached to each sentence saying which kind of data it records.
depth.mechanism: Why do the two channels fail differently, and why can they not be averaged? Start with what each can and cannot reach. Reported data is the only route to experience: the content of a belief, the quality of an auditory experience, the inside of a depressive day. It is limited by articulation, memory, fear and incentive. Observed data is insensitive to cooperation but limited by the clinician's interpretive frame, and the interpretive frame is where the well-documented problems live: the same behaviour read as agitation in one person and as appropriate anger in another, the same flat expression read as blunted affect or as cultural norms of restraint. Merging the channels does two specific kinds of damage. First, it launders an inference into a fact, so 'he was guarded' enters the record as if it had been measured, and every subsequent reader treats it as data. Second, it destroys the diagnostic value of divergence, which is often the most informative signal available: a person stating things are fine while their body tells a different story is a specific and useful pattern, and so is the reverse, where a person describes severe symptoms while appearing untroubled, which may mean anything from excellent support to a different account being given to someone else. The technique of the mechanism is to keep the divergence visible long enough for an explanation to be sought rather than assumed. Its limit is also worth naming: separation does not create validity, and a clinician can produce a beautifully separated note of two unreliable channels, which is why collateral information and repeated observations over time are the only real correctives.
depth.secondExample: Take a fictional assessment of a 70-year-old woman seen at home, where the two channels give divergent answers, and where the correct handling is the opposite of the previous example's. She reports that she is managing well: cooking, cleaning, managing her own affairs. Observed during the visit: the kitchen contains three unopened bags of the same shopping put in different places, she asks twice what day it is, and she cannot find her reading glasses although they are on the table in front of her. The report is warm and confident; the observation is a pattern of repeated purchases and disorientation to date. Here the divergence is not a reason to doubt her honesty, and treating it as such would be both unkind and uninformative. The observed pattern is more consistent with a cognitive change that is being compensated for, and the relevant question is what she does when the compensation fails rather than whether her account can be trusted. Notice that the same technique produces opposite next steps in the two examples: for the 52-year-old man the divergence points to a question about meaning, and for the 70-year-old woman it points to a question about function. The technique does not choose the question; it protects the space in which the right question can be found.
depth.mistake: The classic error is the diagnostic upgrade of an inference. A person who declines a treatment is written up as lacking insight, a person who does not answer questions is written up as paranoid, a person who is angry at a system is written up as hostile. In each case a behaviour that has many possible explanations has been converted into a conclusion about the person's mind, and the conversion is invisible because the conclusion is written in the same grammar as the observation. The correction is mechanical: strike every adjective that names an internal state, then write what was seen and heard underneath it, then decide whether the inference still stands. A second error is to privilege observation because it feels objective, which produces notes in which a person's clear statement of suicidal thoughts is filed beneath an observation that they seemed calm. A third error is silence about divergence, so a reader never learns that the account and the behaviour disagreed. A fourth, specific to writing, is using the person's own words only when they are colourful and paraphrasing them when they are ordinary, which quietly decides in advance which of the person's statements will be treated as evidence. And a fifth is assuming that the absence of an observation is an observation: 'no abnormality noted' on a category that was never assessed is not a finding but a gap dressed as a negative.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Take the blended paragraph given in the example above and rewrite it as a three-part note of no more than 180 words, with each sentence marked R (reported), O (observed) or I (inferred). Then do the harder half: write a second version of the same paragraph for a fictional person whose behaviour and account diverge in the opposite direction, where the person reports severe symptoms and the clinician observes no obvious sign of distress, and state in one sentence what further information would be needed before any inference is drawn. Model response and self-review rubric: a strong first version contains at least four reported items, at least three observations with concrete detail such as timing, posture, speech or content of a gesture, and no more than two inferred items, each with its basis stated. A strong submission uses quotation marks for the person's words and never puts a quotation around a paraphrase. A weak version still contains a sentence such as 'patient appeared disengaged throughout', where nothing in the sentence can be checked by a reader; another weak signal is a note in which every inferred item is also the item that justifies a negative judgement of the person, which is the pattern that lesson 49 on language and iatrogenic harm exists to interrupt.
depth.summary: Assessment produces reported data, observed data and inference, and the three must remain distinguishable in the record. The mental status examination is built on this distinction, dividing mood from affect and instructing the clinician to record mood in the person's own words and to stay neutral when the reported and observed pictures do not align [2]. Merging the channels converts interpretations into facts and destroys the diagnostic value of divergence, which is often the most informative feature of an encounter. Neither channel corrects the other, because they measure different things, which is why the professional response to divergence is to keep it visible and go looking for the explanation over time, with collateral information where it is appropriate. Over-reliance on self-report is one documented route to misdiagnosis and over-trust in observation is the mirror failure, and the discipline that avoids both is the same: say what kind of thing each sentence is.

visual.title: Two-column provenance record with an inference row
visual.description: A page divided into three bands. Top band: reported - the person's words in quotation marks with the time they were said. Middle band: observed - concrete detail of appearance, behaviour, speech and affect, each item stating what was seen or heard rather than what it meant. Bottom band: inferred - marked conclusions, each with the evidence it rests on and a note of what would settle it. A vertical divider separates the encounter timeline from a column for information not obtained.
steps: Reported band: quotation, verbatim, attributed and timed - 'the tablets are doing nothing for me and I want to stop them'.

Observed band: what a camera and microphone would capture - arrived ten minutes early; looked at the floor when treatment was raised; one-sentence answer with a shrug; changed the subject to his daughter's exams.
Divergence line: an explicit statement that report and observation do not align, with no explanation supplied.
Inferred band: the marked conclusion and its basis - topic change when treatment was mentioned may be avoidance or diffidence; unclear which.
Not obtained column: collateral information for the two weeks between appointments; what stopping would mean to him.
Rule box across the foot of the page: mood recorded in the person's words, affect recorded as the clinician's interpretation, no inference written in the grammar of an observation.

lessons.title: Working through an interpreter: the interview with three people in the room
lessons.explanation:
An interpreter-mediated assessment is not the same interview spoken twice. It is a different interaction with different failure modes, and a clinician who treats the interpreter as transparent plumbing will misread the data without ever knowing it. This lesson is education about assessment method. It is not a guide to diagnosing anyone, and the standards cited are professional practice standards for clinicians, not instructions for a reader to apply to a person in their life.

Start with what is actually happening. The clinician hears a rendering, not speech. Everything that reaches the clinician has already been through a second person's understanding, vocabulary and judgement about what matters, and anything the interpreter does not understand cannot be conveyed at all. Interpreting is also not the same as translating: interpreting is spoken and immediate, and equivalence of meaning rather than word-for-word correspondence is the professional standard.

The literature on interpreter use in psychiatry is small and, in the words of one systematic review, insufficient to inform evidence-based guidelines for improving quality of care among patients with limited English proficiency [1]. That sentence is the honest frame for everything that follows, and it is important because the field is full of confident advice. What the same review does report, from the studies it synthesises, is a set of specific distortions. Interpretation errors arise from interpreters' inadequate language proficiency, from lack of psychiatric knowledge that leads an interpreter to normalise disordered speech, from interpreters interjecting their own attitudes or editorial comments, and from interpreters answering on the patient's behalf without asking them at all [1]. Errors were twice as likely to occur when the patient was speaking than when the clinician was, were more likely with acutely psychotic patients, and were especially likely when the patient's replies were long or convoluted, because an interpreter who cannot discern the meaning of a statement may not be able to register and hold it [1]. Compare that with what professional interpreters appear to do well: in one study summarised in the review, care without interpreters was rated as having poor or fair communication in 84 per cent of evaluations, with ad hoc interpreters in 72 per cent, and good in 94 per cent when professional interpreters were used, and the same review reports greater disclosure of traumatic events with professional interpreters than ad hoc interpreters, 77 per cent against 46 per cent [1]. Note the shape of that evidence: it is observational, sample sizes are small, and the review's own conclusion is that the literature cannot support guidelines.

The practical implication runs against convenience. An ad hoc interpreter is anyone not trained in medical interpreting: bilingual staff, friends, relatives, other patients and, in the studies cited, sometimes minors [1]. Using a family member is not a neutral economy. It changes what can be said, because some content is unsayable in front of that person; it changes who is being protected, because the interpreter may soften what is said to protect the relationship; and it puts a third party in a role that carries responsibility without training. NICE's alcohol-use disorders guideline states the professional standard directly: provide independent interpreters, someone not known to the service user, along with written information in an appropriate language [3].

The second structural issue is deciding whether an interpreter is needed at all, and this is where clinicians most often get it wrong in the direction of under-provision. The Victorian Transcultural Psychiatry Unit guidelines set out the reasoning: English proficiency has to be assessed for the task, not for conversation, and a person may be able to hold an everyday conversation while being unable to discuss clinical or emotional content; proficiency can drop during an acute episode; and some affective experiences may only be accessible in the person's first language, because emotional experience is often harder to express in a second language [2]. The guidelines also note that staff easily overestimate a person's English, that proficiency should be re-reviewed over the course of care, and that the presence of delirium, dementia, anxiety, depression or disordered thought further impairs second-language communication [2]. Their proficiency framework is blunt and useful: someone who understands little more than simple greetings needs an interpreter whenever significant information is being elicited or conveyed, and someone who can hold an everyday conversation but not discuss clinical issues or emotional content also needs one [2].

The third issue is what changes about your own technique, and here the guidelines give concrete, testable instructions. Brief the interpreter before the meeting rather than during it. Do not ask an interpreter to translate an assessment instrument sight unseen, because informal translation by an unbriefed interpreter can change the meaning and difficulty of items and yield inaccurate scores; where a formally translated and validated version of an instrument does not exist, the informal translation should be recorded in the notes as informal, with the scores flagged as requiring caution [2]. Review with the interpreter afterwards, and note any doubts about meaning. Offer the person a choice of interpreter where possible, considering sex, age and the implications of religious, ethnic or political differences [2]. And address the person, not the interpreter, which sounds trivial and is the thing interpreters most often report clinicians failing to do.
lessons.example:
A fictional 29-year-old woman who speaks Tigrinya is assessed after her sister brings her to a clinic. She has been sleeping badly, has stopped attending college, and her sister says she has been talking about the neighbours in a way the family does not understand. Two versions of the same 40-minute assessment follow.

Version one. The clinic is busy. A bilingual receptionist who speaks a related language is asked to sit in. She is not trained in interpreting and has never been told what the appointment is about. The clinician asks, through her: 'is she hearing voices?' The receptionist turns to the patient and asks a question. Then she turns back and says: 'she says no, but she is stressed about the neighbours.' The clinician records 'denies auditory hallucinations; preoccupied with neighbours'. Consider what actually happened. The clinician's question went through an untrained adapter; the reply came back as a summary with an evaluative gloss, 'but she is stressed'; the patient's own account, which nobody asked for, is absent from the record; and error probability was highest exactly where the review says it is highest, when the patient speaks at length or her speech is unusual [1]. The note now contains a denial the patient may never have given in those terms.

Version two. A professional interpreter is booked and briefed for five minutes beforehand: the purpose of the meeting, the domains to be covered, the fact that the clinician may ask the same thing in a different way, agreement that the interpreter will render what is said as closely as possible and tell the clinician if something was not understood, and agreement that if the patient's account is unclear the interpreter will say so rather than tidy it up. The clinician uses open questions, keeps sentences short, pauses after each rendering, and looks at the patient while speaking. The patient's reply is longer than expected and contains a phrase the interpreter flags as one she has rendered as 'they are following me', adding that the original word could also mean 'they are watching over me'. That single flagged ambiguity is more clinically informative than the whole of version one, because it identifies exactly where a decision about meaning is being made and by whom. Nothing in the record yet asserts what it means. The clinician also records that the whole encounter was interpreted consecutively by a professional interpreter in the patient's preferred language, that two moments of uncertain rendering were flagged, and that no formally translated version of the mood questionnaire exists in this language, so the questionnaire was not administered rather than administered by informal translation [2].

Now compare the costs. Version two required booking, briefing, an extra five minutes before and ten after, and it produced a note containing explicit uncertainty where version one produced false precision. This is the recurring shape of assessment: the cheaper process produces a cleaner-looking record and a worse one. The systematic review's conclusion that current evidence cannot support guidelines is not a reason to avoid interpreters; it is a reason to prefer the process whose errors are visible [1].
lessons.question: A person's adult daughter offers to interpret, saying she is fluent in both languages and that her mother would prefer it. What is the appropriate response?
lessons.answer: Use an independent professional interpreter where one can be arranged, and if the daughter's help is used for something narrow in an emergency, record exactly what was interpreted by whom, and note the limits this places on the assessment.
lessons.distractor: Accept the offer, because the daughter knows the family best and the mother's stated preference should decide who is in the room, and record the arrangement so that other readers can weigh the information.
lessons.correction: The person's preference about who is present matters, and it does not make the daughter an interpreter: family members are ad hoc interpreters in the sense used in the research, and disclosure with ad hoc interpreters was substantially lower in the studies the review synthesises, with particular losses for sensitive material. The Victorian guidelines are explicit that an interpreter is required regardless of a relative's ability to interpret, except in emergencies, and NICE's guidance states the standard as an independent interpreter who is not known to the service user. The daughter's presence as support is a separate question from her role as conduit, and conflating the two removes the choice that she and her mother are entitled to make.

depth.definitions: Interpreting is the immediate spoken transfer of meaning between languages; translating is the written form; both aim at equivalence of meaning rather than word-for-word correspondence. Consecutive interpreting renders after the speaker finishes; simultaneous or whispered interpreting renders while the speaker continues, and the Victorian guidelines treat the latter with caution because it requires specific training [2]. An ad hoc interpreter is anyone facilitating communication without training in medical interpreting, including bilingual staff, relatives, friends, other patients, and in some studies minors [1]. A professional interpreter is trained and engaged in that role. The proficiency judgement is about the ability to communicate specific clinical and emotional content, not general conversational fluency [2]. An instrument is a questionnaire or rating scale with fixed items; a formally translated instrument is one where translation and validation were carried out as a documented process [2].
depth.mechanism: Why does the presence of a third person change the data rather than merely relaying it? Four mechanisms, each separately documented. First, comprehension loss: anything the interpreter does not understand cannot be conveyed, and the review reports that interpreters may be unable to register and hold a patient's statement when they cannot discern its meaning, with omissions especially likely when replies are long or convoluted [1]. Second, meaning management: an interpreter with psychiatric knowledge who does not understand a disordered statement may normalise it, and an interpreter with relational commitments may soften material to protect the person or the relationship [1]. Third, evaluation: the interpreter becomes a participant who, in some accounts, says what they think the clinician should know, or answers for the patient, and the review documents clinicians' overconfidence in assessments conducted this way [1]. Fourth, the audience effect: disclosure depends on who is present, which is why research comparing professional and ad hoc interpreters found substantially lower disclosure of traumatic material with ad hoc interpreters [1]. The interaction between these mechanisms is what makes the technique matter. Technique cannot eliminate loss; it can make loss visible, by briefing beforehand, by asking for ambiguity to be signalled rather than resolved, and by recording which parts of the encounter were mediated and how. The limit is the state of the evidence: the review's own conclusion is that the literature does not support evidence-based guidelines, so specific claims about which practice is superior are weaker than they sound, and what is best supported is the principle of using trained interpreters rather than untrained ones.
depth.secondExample: Now consider a statutory assessment under mental health legislation, where the decision may concern whether the person is detained, and the person's first language is not the clinician's. The Victorian guidelines list interpreter use as required at assessment including the mental status examination, at risk assessment, when explaining legal rights and changes of status, and when obtaining informed consent [2]. The stakes here expose a distinct failure mode that does not appear in ordinary clinic work: because the interview must be conducted in a suitable manner and the person must understand what is happening to them in order for the process to be fair, a contested rendering is not merely an assessment problem but potentially a legal one. The INforMHAA project in the United Kingdom was set up precisely because its scoping review found an almost total absence of empirical research on interpreter mediation in these assessments and no evidence-based guidance for practice, with the literature treating interpreting as a conduit rather than a collaboration. In practice, the counsel is the same one this lesson gives throughout, applied more strictly: brief, address the person, do not summarise, record who said what, and where a rendering is contested, record the contest. What is different is what rides on getting it wrong.
depth.mistake: The first error is using a relative because it is convenient, which the guidelines explicitly address: an interpreter is required regardless of a relative's ability, except in an emergency, and the person should not be made into an interpreter for their own family member in the other direction either [2]. The second is administering an instrument through informal translation and then reporting the score as though it were a score, when the guidelines say informal translation can change item meaning and difficulty, produce inaccurate numbers, and must be recorded as informal with the scores flagged as cautionary [2]. The third is treating conversational fluency as sufficient: a person who chats easily may be unable to describe emotional experience in English, and proficiency can fall during acute illness [2]. The fourth is the subtle one, which is failing to record that an encounter was mediated. A note that reports the person's statements as though they came from the person, without saying that an interpreter rendered them and without noting ambiguities, hides the mediation from every later reader. The fifth error is treating the interpreter's summary as the person's account and moving on, which loses exactly the material assessment is for.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Write a five-sentence pre-meeting briefing that a clinician could give a professional interpreter before a first assessment, covering purpose, what will be asked and roughly in what order, how you want the interpreting done and what to do with material that is unclear or culturally ambiguous, how the person will be addressed, and what will happen at the end. Then write the four lines of a note recording that the appointment was interpreted: who interpreted, in what language, by what method, what was flagged, and what limits the mediation places on conclusions. Model response and self-review rubric: a strong briefing asks the interpreter to signal ambiguity rather than resolve it, and agrees what the clinician will do when a rendering is disputed. A strong note names the interpreter only as a role, uses no identifying details, states that the account was interpreted rather than spoken in the clinician's language, and records any point where meaning was uncertain. Weak responses include a briefing that starts with clinical content and no logistics, a note that says only 'interpreter present', and any submission in which the interpreter is asked to reassure the person or to explain the clinician's reasoning, which converts the interpreter into a clinician. If your briefing asks the interpreter to give their opinion of whether the person is unwell, delete the sentence: that judgement is not theirs to make and asking for it changes what they will convey.
depth.summary: An interpreter-mediated assessment is a different instrument, not a transparent version of the same one. The clinician receives a rendering, with losses that are largest where speech is long, unusual or emotional, and the evidence base is too thin to support confident prescriptions about practice [1]. What is well supported is the direction of travel: trained interpreters rather than untrained ad hoc ones, independent rather than known to the person [3], a task-based rather than conversational judgement of whether interpretation is needed, instruments administered in formally translated versions or flagged as informal [2], and the person addressed rather than discussed. The technique is to brief before, signal uncertainty during, review after, and record the mediation so that no later reader mistakes a rendering for speech. Precision about who interpreted what, and where meaning was uncertain, is the form that honesty takes here.
