visual.title: The triadic interview: what reaches the clinician and where it is lost
visual.description: Three figures in a row - person, interpreter, clinician - with an arrow from the person to the interpreter labelled 'speech: full account, possibly disorganised, emotionally loaded' and an arrow from the interpreter to the clinician labelled 'rendering: meaning, not words'. Above the middle arrow sit four loss markers, and a side panel lists what the clinician must record.
steps: Loss marker one - comprehension: what the interpreter does not understand is not conveyed, and long or convoluted speech is where omissions cluster.
Loss marker two - normalisation: an interpreter without psychiatric knowledge may tidy disordered speech into ordinary language.
Loss marker three - relational protection: an interpreter who knows the person may soften content to protect the relationship.
Loss marker four - audience effect: what the person is willing to say depends on who is in the room, with lower disclosure reported for untrained interpreters.
Side panel - record: language, who interpreted and in what role, method and setting, points where meaning was flagged as uncertain, whether any instrument was informally translated.
Rule across the diagram: address the person, brief before, review after, and never present a rendering as the person's own words.

lessons.title: Checklists, scales and structured interviews: what they are for, and how they fail
lessons.explanation:
Questionnaires, rating scales and structured diagnostic interviews have a reputation problem in both directions. To some they are the only trustworthy part of psychiatry; to others they are the reduction of a person to a score. Both views are wrong in the same way, because they treat a tool as an answer. This lesson is about what instruments can and cannot do. It contains no diagnostic criteria, no treatment instructions and no advice about any person's care.

Begin with what these instruments are for. A structured instrument fixes the questions and often the order in which they are asked, so that two different clinicians asking the same person at different times have a shared procedure. Rating scales produce numbers on a fixed scale, which makes change over time visible and comparison between services possible. Diagnostic interviews apply decision rules to responses, which is what makes it possible to recruit research samples that are comparable across sites. These are real achievements: the reason structured interviews spread through research and then into clinics is that unstructured interviewing was unreliable, and reliability across raters is not a trivial property.

Now the evidence about what happens when the instrument meets a clinical population. Nordgaard and colleagues compared diagnoses produced by a structured clinical interview administered by a trained non-clinician against consensus lifetime best-estimate diagnoses made by two experienced clinicians who had access to multiple sources including videotaped narrative interviews, in a sample of 100 diagnostically heterogeneous, first-admitted inpatients. The overall agreement was a kappa of 0.18. For schizophrenia the structured interview had a sensitivity of 19 per cent and a specificity of 100 per cent, meaning it missed the great majority of people whom the consensus process considered to have the diagnosis while rarely producing a false positive [1]. The authors conclude that structured interviews performed by non-clinicians are not recommendable for clinical work and should only be used in research with certain precautions [1]. A later replication in 55 first-admitted patients with psychosis found a kappa of 0.21, a sensitivity of 45.5 per cent and specificity of 91 per cent for schizophrenia-spectrum diagnoses, and reported that the structured procedure failed to detect 24 of the 44 patients with such a diagnosis [2]. The replication authors propose three mechanisms for the misdiagnoses: over-reliance on self-report, vulnerability to response set in patients who dissimulate, and a strong diagnosis-and-comorbidity focus in the instrument [2].

Read those numbers carefully, because they do not prove that checklists are useless and they do not prove that clinical judgement is superior. They show that a procedure can be reliable between raters and still agree poorly with a reference standard built from richer information over time. That is the difference between reliability and validity, and it is the single most transferable idea in this lesson. It is also fair to record the other side: the reference standard itself is a consensus judgement rather than an objective truth, the samples are small and drawn from first admissions in specialist settings, and nothing in these studies tests the instruments' use for tracking change in a person already known to a service, which is where most scales are actually employed.

The third finding is a much sharper and more general point about any score. Sensitivity and specificity are properties of a test; what a clinician and the person actually need is the probability that a positive result means the condition is present, and that depends on how common the condition is in the population being tested. Take a screen with 90 per cent sensitivity and 90 per cent specificity. In a population where 1 per cent of people have the condition, out of 10,000 tests you would expect 90 true positives and 990 false positives, so the probability that a positive result is a true case is about 8 per cent: roughly 92 per cent of the positive results are people who do not have the condition [see arithmetic note in the handoff]. If 5 per cent of the population has the condition, the same test gives about 32 per cent. If 40 per cent do, about 86 per cent. The test has not changed; the clinic has. This is why a screening instrument used well in a specialty service can be useless in a general population, and why guideline language matters so much: NICE's depression guideline says to consider using a validated measure to inform and evaluate treatment [3], which is a statement about supporting decisions, not about establishing a diagnosis. It also uses a cut-off as an indicator in defining severity - a score of 16 on a described scale separates the less severe from the more severe category for the purpose of organising treatment - which is a worked example of a line drawn deliberately by a committee for a stated purpose [3].

Finally, the instruments' place in ordinary practice is worth knowing, though the source must be read with care. One review reports that in a survey 72.5 per cent of psychiatrists said they do not use structured interviews in clinical settings, and that constraints on time were the most commonly cited reasons for not using structured interviews [4]. That review is written by the developer of an instrument it presents as an alternative, which is a conflict of interest that should be declared whenever the figure is used. The figure itself is a survey result about practice, not evidence about what works.

A last honest complication: a 2023 retrospective study of 314 patients attending a private clinic for a first visit compared simple closed interview questions on six topics - sleep, sexual problems, marital relationship, parental relationship in childhood, physical abuse and sexual abuse - against validated rating scales for the same domains, and found the questions and scales statistically comparable as predictors, with areas under the curve between 0.74 and 0.92, concluding that an experienced clinician could rely on clinical questions as much as on the scales when symptoms are investigated in general terms [5]. It is a single-site retrospective study and cannot settle the question, but it is the right kind of finding to hold next to the Nordgaard results: instruments and questions trade different errors, and neither is reliable in every setting.
lessons.example:
A fictional community mental health team wants to improve the detection of depression among people referred for other reasons. A trainee proposes that everyone referred should complete a symptom questionnaire and that anyone scoring above a cut-off should be placed on the depression pathway.

Work through the proposal. First, what is the prevalence in the referred population? The team's own figures say about 20 per cent of referrals have a depressive episode that would benefit from the pathway. Using the same illustrative test properties, 90 per cent sensitivity and 90 per cent specificity, at 20 per cent prevalence out of 1,000 people referred you would expect 180 true positives and 80 false positives. That is a workable ratio, and the false positives are not a catastrophe: they are people with something else that the interview gets to look at. Second, what happens if the team applies the same rule to a different population, say all adults registered with the practice, where the prevalence of a current episode is around 5 per cent? Out of 1,000, 45 true positives and 95 false positives, so the probability that a positive result is a true case falls to about 32 per cent. Two-thirds of the people flagged do not have the condition. Third, what does the team do with the score? If the score triggers a same-day decision that the person has depression, the team has converted a screening result into a diagnosis, which the guideline language does not support: it says to consider using a validated measure to inform and evaluate treatment [3]. If the score instead triggers a conversation, and the score is repeated later to see whether things are moving, the team is using the instrument for what it can actually do.

Now add the validity question from the Nordgaard data. Suppose the team also wants to use a structured diagnostic interview to assign diagnoses at referral. The published agreement with a best-estimate standard is around 0.2 kappa, with sensitivity in the 19 to 46 per cent range depending on the study and the diagnosis [1][2]. That does not mean nobody should ever use one. It means that if the team replaces clinical assessment with the instrument, it should expect to miss a large share of cases and should say so in its service evaluation, and that if it keeps the instrument alongside a clinician's assessment and uses disagreement as a signal to look more closely, it is using the tool in the position where it adds rather than substitutes.

Finally, the team should write down what the score cannot do, in the protocol itself, so that the next trainee inherits the reasoning rather than the rule: a score is not a diagnosis, a change in score is not proof that treatment worked, a normal score does not close the question, and the same cut-off cannot be used unchanged in a population with a different prevalence. This paragraph is the deliverable, and it is more useful than any of the numbers.
lessons.question: A service wants to add a screening questionnaire for a condition whose prevalence in its referrals is very low. Using the same test as before, sensitivity 90 per cent and specificity 90 per cent, and a prevalence of 1 per cent, what should the service expect?
lessons.answer: About 92 per cent of the positive results will be people who do not have the condition, so the score can be used to prompt a fuller assessment but cannot be treated as a result in itself.
lessons.distractor: Because specificity is 90 per cent, about 90 per cent of positive results will be correct, and the questionnaire can therefore be reported to users as an accurate test.
lessons.correction: Specificity describes the proportion of people without the condition who test negative; it says nothing directly about the accuracy of a positive result. That quantity depends on prevalence as well as on sensitivity and specificity: with 1 per cent prevalence and 90 per cent sensitivity and specificity, out of 10,000 tests there are 90 true positives and 990 false positives, so about 8 per cent of positives are true cases. The lesson's point is not that the questionnaire is bad but that the same instrument has different meaning in different populations, which is why a validated measure can be appropriate to inform and evaluate treatment in one setting and misleading as a case-finding rule in another.

depth.definitions: A checklist is a fixed list of items to be covered or counted. A rating scale assigns a number to severity or frequency on a defined scale. A structured diagnostic interview fixes questions, sequence and decision rules to generate a diagnosis [1]. Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the condition who test positive; specificity is the proportion without it who test negative. Predictive value is the probability that a person with a given result actually has, or does not have, the condition, and it depends on prevalence as well as on sensitivity and specificity. A cut-off is the score at which a continuous measure is treated as positive. Reliability is agreement between raters or occasions; validity is whether the measure captures what it claims to capture. Tracking a number over time is a different use from making a single decision with that number.
depth.mechanism: Why do instruments with good rater reliability still agree poorly with careful assessment? The mechanisms proposed in the literature are specific rather than general: over-reliance on self-report, response set in people who dissimulate, and a diagnosis-and-comorbidity focus that pushes the interviewer to close categories rather than let a picture emerge [2]. Add the structural mechanism that applies to any fixed instrument: it can only record what it was designed to ask, so a symptom that the instrument does not cover is invisible, and the same instrument asked in a fixed order cannot follow the person's material where it leads. Now the mechanism behind predictive value, which is arithmetic rather than psychological. Sensitivity operates on people who have the condition and specificity on people who do not, but the clinician meets a mixed stream in which the second group is usually far larger. The false positives that specificity generates are therefore multiplied by the size of the larger group, and they swamp the true positives when the condition is uncommon. The practical consequence is that a test's usefulness is a property of the setting, not of the test alone. One important limit on all of this: none of these mechanisms tells you what to do instead, and the studies that measure agreement against a consensus standard cannot show that the alternative would have been better, because the alternative was used to build the standard.
depth.secondExample: Change the setting and the same instrument becomes genuinely useful. Consider a fictional specialist service that sees people already known to have a diagnosis, where a rating scale is administered at every appointment and the score is plotted over time. Here the population is homogeneous and the question is longitudinal rather than categorical: has this person's symptom burden changed since last month? The prevalence problem largely disappears, because the comparison is between two measurements of the same person rather than between a positive result and a population's base rate, and the instrument's fixed wording is now an advantage, because the same words asked in the same way reduce the chance that a change in score reflects a change in interviewer. What the number still cannot do is explain itself. A score that has risen may reflect worsening symptoms, a life event, a change in how the person rates their own experience, or a difference in the context in which the rating was made, and the instrument will not distinguish these. The disciplined use is exactly what the guideline says: use it to inform and evaluate treatment [3], which means the number is one input to a conversation and a decision that also has the person's own account inside it. The transferable contrast with the previous example is that the same tool is informative for tracking within a case and unreliable for deciding whether a case exists.
depth.mistake: The four recurring errors are all modal: they concern what the instrument is being asked to do. The first is treating a cut-off as a diagnosis, so that a score above a threshold is written in the record as the disorder, which converts a probabilistic screening decision into a fact and bypasses the assessment that the guideline language asks for [3]. The second is treating a reliable tool as a valid one, which is the error the Nordgaard data speaks to directly: high agreement between raters using the same instrument does not mean the instrument measures what it is supposed to measure [1]. The third is counting symptoms rather than weighing meaning, which produces records in which eleven criteria are listed and nothing is said about what the experiences are like, how long they have lasted, in what context they began, or what the person makes of them; NIMH's own research framework notes that using symptom counts to divide people into well and ill groups can obscure how psychopathology emerges gradually across development. The fourth is changing instrument mid-course, which destroys the tracking value that was the reason for using one. A fifth, less obvious error, is applying a cut-off derived in one population to another without adjusting the interpretation, which is the arithmetic failure demonstrated above.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. A fictional service tells you its referral population has an expected prevalence of 5 per cent for the condition of interest and that it plans to use a screen with 90 per cent sensitivity and 90 per cent specificity. 1) Work out, showing your arithmetic, how many true and false positives you would expect per 1,000 people screened, and what proportion of positive results would be true cases. 2) Write three sentences telling the service what the screen can and cannot be used for. 3) Then answer in one paragraph: if the service instead applied the screen only to a much smaller group already thought to be at high risk, with a prevalence of 40 per cent, what would change, and what would not change about the test itself? Model response and self-review rubric: a strong answer states the arithmetic explicitly - 45 true positives and 95 false positives per 1,000, so about 32 per cent of positives are true cases - and then states that the screen may prompt assessment but may not be reported as establishing the condition. A strong third answer notes that neither sensitivity nor specificity changes when prevalence changes, and that only the interpretation of a positive result changes, which is why the same instrument can be described as accurate in one setting and unreliable in another without contradiction. Weak answers describe a positive result as 90 per cent accurate, fail to distinguish sensitivity from predictive value, or propose that the service should stop screening altogether, which does not follow from the arithmetic.
depth.summary: Instruments are reliable procedures with limited validity, and their usefulness depends on what they are being asked to do and where they are being used. Fixed questions and fixed scales buy agreement between raters and the ability to see change over time, at the cost of everything the instrument does not ask and everything a person does not say in response to it. The published agreement between a structured diagnostic interview and a best-estimate standard in first-admission samples is poor, with sensitivities reported between 19 and 46 per cent, and the mechanisms proposed are over-reliance on self-report, response sets and a category-closing focus [1][2]. Sensitivity and specificity do not tell you the probability that a positive result is a true case; prevalence does, and it can make the same test useful or useless. NICE's language - use a validated measure to inform and evaluate treatment - is the correct register [3], and a single retrospective study suggesting that simple closed questions can rival scales for general screening should be held as a complication rather than a verdict [5]. The discipline is to write down, in the protocol, which job each instrument is doing.

(2012), "Assessing the diagnostic validity of a structured psychiatric interview in a first-admission hospital sample", World Psychiatry 11(3): 181-185 - read the abstract and the results for the kappa agreement and the sensitivity and specificity figures, and the concluding paragraph

Note the sample size and the specialist setting before generalising, and note that the comparison standard is itself a judgement rather than a gold truth.

Open access and read in full. Its earlier-sample detail on denial and partial disclosure is used in lessons 63 and 65.

Read it as a statement about the role of measurement in a pathway, not as criteria for diagnosis. The guideline is for England and Northern Ireland; other jurisdictions have their own.

Declare the conflict of interest when citing it: the paper is written by the developer of the alternative instrument it describes, so its framing of existing tools is not neutral. Included deliberately as a complication of the lesson's argument rather than as support for using questions instead of instruments.

visual.title: What a score can and cannot tell you: the prevalence pump
visual.description: A two-panel figure. Left panel: the same test - sensitivity 90 per cent, specificity 90 per cent - applied to two populations, one with 1 per cent prevalence and one with 40 per cent prevalence, showing true and false positives per 10,000 people as stacked bars. Right panel: a checklist of roles, with tick or cross against each.
steps: Population A, 1 per cent prevalence: 90 true positives and 990 false positives, so roughly 8 per cent of positive results are true cases.
Population B, 5 per cent prevalence: 450 true positives and 950 false positives, so roughly 32 per cent of positive results are true cases.
Population C, 40 per cent prevalence: 3,600 true positives and 600 false positives, so roughly 86 per cent of positive results are true cases.
Note under the bars: sensitivity and specificity have not changed; only the mix of people has.
Role tick: supported - covering a fixed list of domains, producing a number that can be compared over time, prompting a fuller assessment.
Role cross: not supported - establishing a diagnosis, closing a question because the score is normal, carrying a cut-off unchanged into a population with a different prevalence.

questions.prompt: A fictional trainee is asked to cut a first assessment from 60 to 30 minutes. She proposes keeping the opening, the structured symptom list and the risk questions, and dropping the narrative phase and the closing summary. A supervisor says the resulting interview will be cheaper to run and harder to read. What is the supervisor identifying?
questions.answer: Without the narrative there is no basis for choosing which focused questions matter, and without the summary there is no chance for the person to correct the account, so the record will contain coverage that cannot be argued with.
questions.distractor: The proposal breaks the required order of an assessment, because the symptom list may only be completed after a closing summary has been read back and agreed.
questions.correction: There is no required order in that sense: the phase sequence is a design choice with costs, and services do reorder it, for instance in crisis settings where physical causes and immediate needs come first. The supervisor's point is about what each phase supplies. Nordgaard and colleagues' argument that information is sometimes obtained only by not asking for it directly is an argument for breadth before depth, and the closing summary is where corrections appear; a 30-minute interview that keeps both can work, while one that keeps neither produces a document in which nothing could have been corrected.

questions.prompt: A fictional note reads: 'Presented as a 24-year-old man, unkempt, hostile, minimising, clearly substance-affected, poor insight.' A second clinician says she cannot tell what happened in the appointment. Using the reported-observed-inferred discipline, which correction best repairs the note?
questions.answer: Keep the concrete descriptions that could be checked - what he wore and how he spoke, what he actually said, in his words - and mark the judgements such as hostile or poor insight as inferences with the evidence they rest on, or remove them.
questions.distractor: Translate every judgement into a standard mental status term, so that hostile becomes guarded affect and unkempt becomes reduced self-care, which converts the impressions into the technical language of the examination.
questions.correction: Renaming an impression in clinical vocabulary does not turn it into an observation; it makes it harder to dispute because it now looks like a category rating. The mental status examination keeps mood and affect apart precisely so that one is recorded in the person's words and the other as the clinician's interpretation with descriptive detail, and it instructs neutrality rather than resolution when the reported and observed pictures disagree. Marking the judgements as judgements, with their basis or their absence, is the repair that gives the next reader something to weigh.

questions.prompt: A fictional 61-year-old woman has attended three appointments in English, chatting easily about her grandchildren, and has been assessed as not needing interpreting support. At the fourth appointment her daughter reports that her mother has been unable to describe her low mood in any language for two weeks and has stopped mentioning the nightmares. What does this sequence illustrate?
questions.answer: That conversational fluency is a poor test of the ability to discuss clinical and emotional content, and that proficiency should be judged against the task and reviewed again as the person's state changes.
questions.distractor: That the daughter should be asked to interpret from now on, since she is the person best placed to know what her mother is unable to express.
questions.correction: The guidelines on working with interpreters separate everyday conversation from the ability to discuss clinical information and emotional content, note that some affective experiences may only be accessible in a person's first language, and state that proficiency can fall during acute illness and should be re-reviewed. Using a relative is exactly the ad hoc arrangement the evidence associates with lower disclosure of sensitive material, and it also removes the choice the person is entitled to make about who is in the room.

questions.prompt: A fictional service decides that anyone scoring below a set cut-off on a symptom questionnaire at two consecutive appointments will be discharged from its depression pathway. A staff member objects. Which objection is best supported?
questions.answer: The score has a defined role in informing and evaluating treatment rather than in establishing who has the condition, and its meaning depends on how common the condition is among the people being screened, so a cut-off cannot carry that decision on its own.
questions.distractor: Questionnaires cannot be used in services at all, because the research shows that structured instruments agree poorly with consensus assessment and therefore have no clinical role.
questions.correction: The guideline position is that a validated measure can be considered to inform and evaluate treatment, which is a supporting role rather than a decision rule. The agreement studies concern structured diagnostic interviews, a different instrument used for a different job, and they report poor agreement with a best-estimate standard in small first-admission samples rather than demonstrating that scales have no role. The strongest objection is the arithmetic one: sensitivity and specificity do not fix the probability that a given result is correct, and that probability falls sharply when the condition is uncommon in the population screened.

questions.prompt: A fictional team with severe staffing shortages proposes replacing all new assessments with a structured diagnostic interview administered by an administrative assistant, keeping a clinician for a brief review of each completed instrument. Which reply most accurately describes what the team is buying?
questions.answer: Greater consistency in what is asked and in how it is recorded, at the cost of validity: published agreement between such instruments and best-estimate diagnosis in first-admission samples is poor, with sensitivities reported between roughly 19 and 46 per cent.
questions.distractor: Greater validity, because a fixed sequence of questions removes the clinician's own bias from the assessment, which is the source of disagreement between assessors.
questions.correction: Fixed procedures reduce variability between assessors, which is reliability, and reliability is not validity. The Nordgaard study reported kappa 0.18 with 19 per cent sensitivity and 100 per cent specificity against a consensus standard, and the replication reported kappa 0.21 with 45.5 per cent sensitivity, meaning a large share of cases were missed. Removing the clinician's judgement also removes the channel through which dissimulation is noticed; the replication names over-reliance on self-report as one proposed mechanism of misdiagnosis.

units.title: Difficult questions, contested concepts and the written record

lessons.title: Asking about suicide plainly: euphemism, pace, and the limits of prediction
lessons.explanation:
This lesson is about how clinicians ask a question, and about what risk assessment can and cannot do. It is education only. It contains no method for assessing anyone, no risk-scoring instructions, and nothing that should be used to judge your own safety or another person's. If you are worried about a person in your life, or about yourself, the useful step is to contact local emergency or crisis services rather than to apply anything you read here.

The first point is linguistic. Clinicians hedge, and hedging costs information. Euphemisms - 'you're not having any bad thoughts?', 'no thoughts of doing anything silly?', 'you're not planning anything, are you?' - do several things at once: they communicate discomfort, they signal the expected answer, and they leave the person free to answer a different question from the one intended. The National Institute of Mental Health's public guidance takes the opposite approach, putting the words in a direct form: the first of its five steps is ASK - 'Are you thinking about suicide?' - and it notes that this is not an easy question to ask but can help start a conversation [1]. Note what that sentence does and does not claim. It does not claim that any particular wording is validated. It claims that a direct question opens a conversation, which is the purpose. The related question - whether asking increases distress - has been studied; in a study of adolescents who had previously received inpatient psychiatric care, repeated assessment of suicidal ideation over up to two years was followed by a significant decline in reported ideation rather than an increase, and the authors conclude that asking an at-risk population about suicidal ideation is not associated with subsequent increases [2]. That is evidence about research assessment in one population, and it is the strongest available answer to a question clinicians ask constantly. It is not proof about every wording in every setting.

The second point is that a question is not an assessment. Asking plainly is the beginning of an inquiry whose shape should be: what is the person thinking about, how often, how long has it been going on, what makes it worse and what holds it back, what has changed recently, what has helped before, what the person wants right now, and who else knows. Notice that this is closer to the narrative phase of lesson 61 than to a scoring exercise, and that its purpose is to understand a person rather than to derive a category.

On that last word - category - the evidence is unusually clear, and it runs against practice that is still common. NICE's guidance on self-harm states plainly that risk assessment tools and scales should not be used to predict future suicide or repetition of self-harm, that they should not be used to determine who should and should not be offered treatment or who should be discharged, and that global risk stratification into low, medium or high risk should not be used either to predict or to determine access to care [3]. The guidance's stated rationale is that the tools cannot accurately predict risk, that stratification implies a static risk where risk is dynamic, and that determining access to treatment with inaccurate tools can lead to repeat self-harm, distress and poorer experience of care, with care instead determined by needs and safety [4]. What the guidance does require is that a risk formulation is undertaken as part of every psychosocial assessment [3]. That is a substitution, not a downgrade: the formulation is the partly argued, revisable document described in lesson 51, applied to risk, and its content is needs, triggers and planned actions rather than a label.

Why can prediction not be delivered? Three reasons, all structural rather than fixable. Suicide is rare enough that even a test with good sensitivity and specificity produces mostly false positives, which is the arithmetic of lesson 65 applied to an outcome with a very low base rate. Most of the strongest statistical predictors are common - being male, being older, having a history of self-harm - so they identify large groups in which almost nobody will die. And the measurement itself is unstable: a person's state changes hour to hour, so a rating taken at four in the afternoon says little about the following week. The guidance also notes that suicide rates after an episode of self-harm are higher in older people, which is the kind of pattern-level observation that belongs in a formulation rather than in a score [3].

What follows practically is a different kind of competence. Ask plainly and early. Ask about what the person is actually experiencing rather than repeating a formula. Listen for the needs underneath, which may include pain, debt, housing, a relationship, a physical illness, or an unbearable sense of being a burden. Take the person's own account of what has changed seriously without treating it as either a prophecy or a performance. Write what was discussed and what was agreed, with a review date. And accept the uncomfortable professional position that the point of the work is not to convert a person into a manageable risk category, but to keep a conversation going in which the person's own reasons for living and dying can be spoken about.
lessons.example:
A fictional 33-year-old man attends a general practice appointment for an unrelated reason. He mentions in passing that he has not been sleeping and that his business is failing. Two versions of what happens next.

Version one. The clinician hears the words, feels a jolt, and asks whether he is 'having any thoughts like that'. He says no. The clinician asks whether he would ever act on anything like that, and he says no. The appointment moves on, and the note records that he denied suicidal ideation. Consider the exchange as information. The clinician's question was vague enough that 'thoughts like that' could mean anything, the second question was a leading question of an intimidating kind, and the moment at which the person mentioned the failing business was the moment to stay with rather than to close. The note is also doing something risky: 'denied suicidal ideation', written after two hedged questions, is a statement the record presents as a finding.

Version two. The clinician stays with it, and uses plain words: 'when people tell me they can't sleep and everything is falling apart, I usually ask directly. Are you thinking about suicide?' The man pauses and says yes, some days, and then says he would not do anything because of his daughter. The clinician asks what the days are like, what makes them worse, whether he has taken any steps towards anything, what has kept him here so far, whether his brother knows, and what he wants from today. Nothing is decided in this appointment except one thing: he will be seen again in four days, and the two of them agree what he will do in between if the days get worse, including who he can call. The note records what he said, in his words, what was agreed, and that a fuller assessment will follow. Risk is not scored. Nothing has been 'ruled out', and the record does not pretend otherwise.

Now compare what the two documents do. The first records a categorical denial that is worth very little, and it will be read by the next clinician as reassurance. The second records an account with a moving part in it - some days yes, the daughter as a reason to stay - and it names the continuing uncertainty and the review date. The second is harder to write, because it refuses to convert a person into a category. It is also the one that keeps a conversation available, which is what the plain question was for. Note what the clinician did not do in either version: no detailed enquiry about methods, no explicit means specifics in the record, and no attempt to establish a numerical level of risk, because the prediction literature does not support it and the record should not pretend to a precision that does not exist.
lessons.question: A fictional team is required by its manager to record a numerical suicide risk level for every patient, on the grounds that it makes thresholds for further input transparent. What is the strongest response?
lessons.answer: The guidance advises against using tools, scales or global risk stratification either to predict suicide or to determine access to treatment, and instead requires a risk formulation that names needs, the situations in which risk would rise, and planned actions, with review.
lessons.distractor: A numerical level is acceptable if it is derived from clinical judgement rather than from a scale, because the objection is to instruments rather than to the idea of recording a level of risk.
lessons.correction: The recommendation is not limited to scores: NICE states that global risk stratification into low, medium or high risk should not be used to predict suicide or repetition of self-harm, and should not be used to determine who is offered treatment or who is discharged. The stated rationale is that such tools cannot accurately predict, that stratification presents risk as static when it is dynamic, and that arbitrary thresholds reduce access to care. A clinical judgement expressed as a level inherits the same problems, whereas a formulation can carry the uncertainty and the contingency that a level cannot.

depth.definitions: Suicidal ideation is thinking about ending one's own life, with or without a plan; self-harm is intentional self-injury or self-poisoning, which may or may not carry intent to die; these overlap and are not interchangeable. A risk formulation is a documented account of a person's needs, the situations in which risk of self-harm or suicide would increase, and proposed actions to reduce it, undertaken as part of a psychosocial assessment [3]. A risk assessment tool or scale is an instrument that produces a score or category intended to quantify risk. Global risk stratification is the placement of a person into a low, medium or high category. Base rate is how common an outcome is in the population of interest, and it is the reason predictive values behave differently from sensitivities. A safety plan is a written, jointly agreed plan for what to do if things worsen, referenced in the guidance as something developed with and agreed by the person rather than imposed on them [3].
depth.mechanism: Why can a formulation be required while prediction is discouraged? Because they answer different questions. Prediction asks what will happen to this person, and it fails for structural reasons: the base rate is very low, the strongest risk factors are so common that they identify vast groups containing almost no deaths, the person's state is unstable across days and hours, and much of the information depends on what a person chooses to disclose. Formulation asks what is happening to this person and what can be done about it in the next interval, and failure modes there are different - a formulation can omit a need or misjudge a priority, and it can be revised. The mechanism of the substitution is therefore that the profession has changed the question it can answer honestly. Note the second mechanism behind the plain question: euphemism does not merely fail to elicit information, it actively shapes the answer by communicating a preferred response and by modelling discomfort, which means that a bare denial obtained through a hedged question carries almost no information. A direct question removes the ambiguity about what is being asked, which is why the public guidance puts the words directly. The evidence limit on both mechanisms should be stated: the studies behind 'asking does not increase distress' concern specific populations and repeated research assessment [2], and no instrument has been shown to predict individual outcomes in a way that supports the thresholds services once used [4].
depth.secondExample: Consider a fictional 72-year-old woman brought to an emergency department after taking an overdose of her own pain medication; she tells the assessing clinician that she does not want to talk about it and asks to go home. Here the usual trap is chronological: the clinician, under time pressure and on the receiving end of a clear wish to leave, may ask one closed question, record a denial, and let the assessment be completed later. NICE's guidance anticipates exactly this pressure and states that if a person who has self-harmed presents to services but wants to leave before a full psychosocial assessment has taken place, immediate risks, mental capacity and any mental health problems should be assessed before they leave [3]. Notice what this instruction does: it does not require the full conversation to happen against the person's will, and it does not permit the question to be skipped. It also sits alongside the guidance's observation that suicide rates after an episode of self-harm are higher in older people [3]. The technique in this case is to say plainly what happens next: that the conversation matters, that the person may decline parts of it, and that a plan for the immediate interval will be made with her rather than for her. The discomfort of a person who does not want to talk is not a reason to make the question easier; it is a reason to make it plainer and to explain why it is being asked.
depth.mistake: The first error is the euphemism, which is often defended as kindness and is usually the clinician's own discomfort being managed at the person's expense. The second is treating a denial as an all-clear: a no after a leading question is evidence about the question, and the assertion in a note that a person 'denied suicidal ideation' invites exactly the wrong inference. The third is shifting from asking about experience to asking about prediction, which happens when the conversation turns to what the person thinks they might do in the future; that question presses a person to forecast a state they cannot forecast, and it often produces a reassuring answer that then sits in the record as a reassurance. The fourth is producing a risk category and letting it substitute for a formulation, which the guidance specifically discourages, because the category presents risk as static and can shut the door on the very care the person needs [4]. A fifth error is less obvious and more serious: responding to a disclosure with a plan the person has not agreed to, which removes what agency they still have at the moment they are most stripped of it. A sixth is the mirror failure at the other end, in which fear drives the clinician to ask about methods in detail, which neither improves the plan nor helps the person, and which fills the record with material that adds no protective value. The correct register is plain, unhurried, and specific about what happens next.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Write two short paragraphs of a fictional clinical interaction. In the first, show a question about suicide asked in a way that a reader could criticise, and write one sentence identifying what the wording did. In the second, show the same moment rewritten plainly, and then write a four-line risk formulation for that fictional person: needs identified, situations in which risk would increase, actions proposed, and review date. Do not include any method detail anywhere in your answer. Model response and self-review rubric: a strong pair of paragraphs shows that the criticised wording was not merely crude but strategically bad, because it signalled the expected answer and made a denial meaningless. A strong formulation names concrete needs and triggers - for instance debt, sleep loss, an anniversary, a specific conflict - rather than restating diagnoses, and it ends with a date. A weak formulation says the person is at low, medium or high risk, or asserts that the person is not at risk because they denied intent, or claims a level of precision no instrument can supply. A submission that includes any method information should be rewritten to describe the person's experience instead; that information does not improve a plan and does not belong in a record.
depth.summary: Asking about suicide is a piece of technical skill with a plain-words core: direct questions, the person's own account of their experience, and a refusal to convert ambivalence into a forecast. The published guidance is unusually firm on what not to do - no tools or scales to predict, no low-medium-high stratification to predict or to ration care - and it requires instead a risk formulation covering needs, triggers and actions as part of every psychosocial assessment [3][4]. Prediction fails for structural reasons that no clinician can overcome: a very low base rate, risk factors too common to discriminate, and an unstable measured state. What remains is harder and more useful: keep the question plain, keep the conversation open, name the person's reasons for staying alive as well as their reasons for dying, record what was agreed and when it will be reviewed, and be honest in writing that a no obtained through a hedge is not an answer.

lessons.title: Insight: a contested concept and its clinical consequences
lessons.explanation:
Few words in psychiatry carry more unexamined moral weight than insight. 'Poor insight' in a record can mean that a person does not accept a diagnosis, or that they do not believe anything is wrong at all, or that they disagree with a plan, or that they were angry in the appointment, and the four are not the same finding. This lesson examines the concept, its evidence and its contested edges. It is education about how clinicians describe people, not a method for judging anyone's self-understanding, and it contains no treatment instructions.

The history is instructive because the term began as something more precise than it is today. Pick in 1882, as reported in the review cited below, defined insight as a person's recognition of the pathological aspect of their mental processes, and treated it as varying in degree, with the weakest form described as an illness-feeling and the strongest as full illness-insight involving conscious reflection [1]. Lewis in 1934, again as the review reports him, defined insight into mental illness as a correct attitude to a morbid change in oneself and characterised it as a matter of judgment, achievable by inference from what he called secondary evidence of change in oneself, such as a lessened capacity [1]. Two things follow from those definitions. First, insight was always understood as graduated rather than present or absent. Second, it was a judgement about a change in the person's own functioning, which is a narrower question than whether the person agrees with a psychiatric classification.

Contemporary work splits the concept, and the split is worth knowing because clinicians use the two senses interchangeably. Clinical insight refers to awareness of having a mental illness, the ability to relabel experiences as symptoms, awareness of the need for treatment and awareness of the psychosocial consequences; cognitive insight refers to the capacity for self-reflection and the ability to resist excessive certainty about one's own conclusions, measured separately [1][2]. A person can be high on one and low on the other, which alone refutes any single rating.

The evidence about consequences is more interesting than the folk version. The review reports that poor insight predicts poorer treatment adherence and weaker therapeutic alliance, higher symptom severity and more impaired community function [1]. That is the version clinicians expect. But the same review reports the opposite pattern for good insight: good clinical insight is associated with depression and poorer self-reported quality of life, a pattern that earlier research named the insight paradox, and later studies have found good insight to be correlated with depression and related constructs, with evidence that good insight prospectively predicted higher demoralisation and that improvements in insight were linked to increases in depressive symptoms in first-episode psychosis and acute schizophrenia [1]. The review also notes that clinical and cognitive insight have been identified as potential risk factors for suicide in the sense of being associated with higher measured suicidality in some samples [1]. Handle that last finding soberly and accurately: it is a correlational association between measured insight and measured suicidality in particular samples, not a prediction about any individual, and it does not license either lowering someone's awareness or ignoring the finding. What it does undermine is the assumption that more insight is simply better.

Why would that be so? The review's integrative model offers a mechanism rather than a moral. Insight, on this account, requires integrating information about changes in one's internal states, external circumstances, other people's perspectives and one's life trajectory, together with the causes and consequences of each; and the emotionally difficult content is exactly what has to be integrated [1]. A person who has taken that work in may be more aware of loss, more exposed to stigma, and more accurate about a future they did not choose. The review also lists the roots of poor insight as plural rather than singular: biological, experiential, neuropsychological, social-cognitive, metacognitive and socio-political factors [1]. That plurality is the strongest argument against treating insight as a personality defect or a failure of will.

The measurement side is where the concept becomes visibly unstable. A 2025 systematic review of instruments for assessing insight in psychosis, conducted against a formal psychometric framework, states in its abstract that insight is a multidimensional construct involving awareness of illness, attribution of symptoms and perceived need for treatment, and that substantial variability in how insight is conceptualised and measured continues to hinder clinical assessment and cross-study comparisons; it also reports that differences between self-report and clinician ratings were common and often clinically meaningful [2]. Read together with the earlier review, the position is clear: insight is a useful clinical idea, its content depends on which question is being asked, its instruments do not agree with each other or across raters and observers, and the direction of its relationship to wellbeing is not one-directional.

Two ethical consequences follow, and both are practical. First, because the concept is contested and its measurement unstable, a bare assertion of poor insight in a record should be replaced by the specific content: what does this person say about whether anything has changed, what do they attribute their experiences to, what do they think about the treatment that has been offered, and what do they think will happen. Second, and more important, insight is not capacity. Disagreeing with a diagnosis, or holding an unusual explanation for one's experiences, is not the same as being unable to understand, retain, weigh or communicate a decision, which is the legal test set out in lesson 53. A person may be judged to lack insight on any of these scales and still have full decision-making capacity, and a clinician who lets the first judgement leak into the second has made a legal error, not merely a conceptual one.
lessons.example:
Four fictional people, all described by different clinicians as having 'poor insight'.

The first is a 27-year-old man who has been given a diagnosis after a first episode of psychosis. He accepts that something is wrong and takes the treatment offered, but he says the explanation is not right: he describes his experiences as spiritual rather than symptomatic, and he says his family's distress followed the experiences rather than causing them. He is adherent, engaged and articulate. Call his clinical insight partial on the awareness dimension, low on the attribution dimension, and high on the dimension of need for treatment.

The second is a 45-year-old woman who says nothing is wrong, resists all contact, and after six months of persuasion attends once. She cannot say what would count as evidence that anything is wrong and has no account of her circumstances other than that people are interfering with her. Call her low across the dimensions.

The third is a 19-year-old man who describes his difficulties accurately, complains that they are destroying his life, and reads everything he can find about the diagnosis; he is also unshakably certain that his own interpretation is correct and dismisses anything that contradicts it. His clinical insight is high and his cognitive insight - the capacity to consider that he might be wrong - is low.

The fourth is a 60-year-old woman who agrees with every formulation offered, says she has a serious illness, accepts the plan without question, and has clearly not understood the plan at all; when asked what she has agreed to, her answer is unrelated. Here calling her 'insightful' would be the error: agreement is not understanding, and the relevant assessment is of her capacity to understand and retain the information, which is lesson 53's territory rather than this one's.

Now notice what happens if a service records a single insight rating for all four. The rating collapses four different situations: a dispute about explanation with full engagement; an apparent lack of recognition; high awareness with low self-reflection; and apparent agreement without comprehension. Each points towards a different next step, and none of them is a statement about the person's worth or their capacity. The exercise transfers to writing: the question to ask of any note containing the word insight is what the person actually said, on which dimension, and what evidence supports the rating.
lessons.question: A fictional assessment records 'poor insight' as a single global rating for a person who accepts the diagnosis and takes the treatment but thinks the explanation offered is wrong. What is the main problem with this recording?
lessons.answer: It collapses distinct dimensions into one label: awareness of illness, attribution of experiences, recognition of the need for treatment and awareness of consequences are separate, and self-report and clinician ratings commonly diverge, so the rating says less than the note implies.
lessons.distractor: The problem is that insight cannot be assessed by a clinician at all, because only the person can report their own awareness, so any clinician rating is a fabrication.
lessons.correction: Clinician-rated and self-report measures both exist and they often disagree, which is why the systematic review of instruments describes the variability as a hindrance to clinical assessment and cross-study comparisons rather than a reason to abandon the concept. The defensible practice is to state the dimension and the evidence, for example whether the person thinks anything has changed, what they attribute their experiences to, and what they want to do about it. A single label also invites the second and more serious error, which is letting it do the work that legally belongs to a capacity assessment.

depth.definitions: Clinical insight is awareness of having a mental illness, the ability to relabel experiences as symptoms, recognition of the need for treatment and awareness of the psychosocial consequences [1][2]. Cognitive insight is the capacity for self-reflection and resistance to excessive certainty, measured on a separate instrument with distinct subscales [1][2]. The insight paradox is the reported association between good insight and depression, demoralisation and lower self-reported quality of life [1]. Demoralisation in this literature names a state of discouragement and loss of morale rather than a diagnosis. An illness-feeling is Pick's weakest grade of insight, a sense that something is not right rather than a formulated understanding [1]. Capacity is a legal test about understanding, retaining, weighing and communicating a specific decision, and it is not the same question as insight, as lesson 53 sets out.
depth.mechanism: Why should awareness of illness be associated with worse mood, when awareness sounds like the goal? The integrative model answers with a mechanism about integration rather than acceptance [1]. On this account insight requires combining information about changes in one's internal states, external circumstances, other people's perspectives and one's life trajectory, along with the causes and consequences of each; the material to be integrated is often painful, and its integration is not a matter of agreeing to a label. The review lists the roots of poor insight as biological, experiential, neuropsychological, social-cognitive, metacognitive and socio-political, which means the same rating can arise from a cognitive impairment, a defence against unbearable content, a different cultural explanation of experience, or a rational response to stigma and discrimination. That plurality also explains why instruments disagree: they ask different questions and presuppose different aetiologies. Two limits should be stated. First, almost all of this evidence is correlational, from samples defined by diagnosis, so it cannot establish that insight causes depression or that anything should be done differently. Second, the association with suicidality in some samples is exactly the kind of finding that must not be read backwards into practice: awareness is not a harm to be managed by keeping a person uninformed, and the review's own reading is that the appropriate response is helping people integrate difficult experience into a coherent personal account [1].
depth.secondExample: Now take the concept out of a psychosis clinic, which is where nearly all of the literature sits, and apply it to a fictional 52-year-old man with a long-standing alcohol problem who says he drinks because of stress and that he could stop whenever he chooses, and to a fictional 34-year-old woman who has been told she has an anxiety disorder and who accepts the diagnosis but insists her difficulties are caused by her employer's behaviour and are therefore not an illness at all. In the first case a clinician may write 'poor insight', and the useful content is different: does he think his drinking has consequences, does he connect it with his sleep and his liver results, and does he see any reason to change? In the second, the same phrase would be used for a person who agrees she has the symptoms but disputes the framing, which is an argument about explanation rather than a failure to perceive anything, and one she may be right about in part, since the employment situation is real. The transferable technique is the same in both: convert the global rating into the specific questions, ask them separately, and then note the answers rather than the verdict. Note the asymmetry this exposes in the standard instruments: they were developed in samples with psychotic disorders and their items assume a medical frame, so applying them unchanged to a dispute about explanation in another presentation is a category error rather than a measurement.
depth.mistake: The first error is writing an insight rating with no content, which leaves every later reader to fill the gap with their own assumptions. The second is treating a dispute about explanation as a disease feature: a person who attributes their experiences to a religious, political or social cause may be wrong, but calling that poor insight converts a disagreement into a symptom, and the literature's own inclusion of socio-political factors among the roots of poor insight should make a clinician cautious about doing so [1]. The third is the reverse error, treating agreement as insight: a person who agrees with everything may be deferring, may be unable to follow the discussion, or may be saying what shortens the appointment, and the 2025 review's finding that self-report and clinician ratings diverge in clinically meaningful ways is a warning about both directions [2]. The fourth is using insight as a proxy for capacity, which is a legal mistake as well as a conceptual one; the fifth is using the paradox finding to justify withholding information, which is not supported by the evidence and would be a serious ethical failure. A sixth, quieter error is using the phrase in the spoken interview as an accusation - asking a person whether they accept that they are unwell, in a tone that presupposes the answer - which produces compliance rather than information.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Write four separate one-line questions that between them cover awareness of change, attribution of experience, perceived need for treatment, and awareness of consequences, each phrased so that a person could answer in a way that contradicts the clinician without provoking an argument. Then write a fictional note of no more than 80 words describing a person's insight without using the words insight, insightless or unwell, and without any global rating. Finally, rewrite one of your four questions as it would sound if it were asked as an accusation, and state in one sentence what it would elicit instead. Model response and self-review rubric: a strong question about attribution invites the person's own explanation before the clinician's, for example asking what they think has been happening and what they make of it. A strong note records each dimension with the person's words and marks the clinician's inference as inference. A weak note smuggles a global rating back in through synonyms such as 'does not acknowledge difficulties' or 'lacks awareness of the nature of his problems', neither of which names what was said. A weak set of questions contains at least one question whose only reasonable answer is yes, which is the pattern that produces the compliance the lesson warns about. If your rewritten accusatory question sounds like the questions in your first list, revise until the difference is audible.
depth.summary: Insight is a clinical idea with a specific history, at least two contemporary senses, and an evidence base whose most striking finding runs against intuition: poor insight is associated with poorer adherence and function, and good insight is associated with depression, demoralisation and lower self-reported quality of life, with an association in some samples between higher insight and higher measured suicidality [1]. The concept is contested on its own terms: instruments for assessing it conceptualise it differently, self-report and clinician ratings commonly diverge in clinically meaningful ways, and the roots proposed for poor insight include cognitive, experiential, social-cognitive, metacognitive and socio-political factors rather than a single deficiency [1][2]. What this licenses in writing is specificity: say which dimension, record what the person said, and refuse the global label. What it does not license is using insight as a synonym for capacity, or as a reason to keep someone less informed.
