lessons.title: Distress and disorder: where the line is drawn, by whom, and what it costs
lessons.explanation:
Everyone suffers. Not everyone has a disorder. The distinction matters because resources, records, treatments and stigma all attach to it, and because the line is drawn by committees rather than discovered in nature. This lesson examines how the boundary is defined, what purposes it serves and what it costs. It is education about classification and its consequences, not a means of deciding whether any particular person's suffering qualifies as an illness.

Begin with the definition in use. The World Health Organization's fact sheet states that a mental disorder is characterised by a clinically significant disturbance in an individual's cognition, emotional regulation, or behaviour, and that it is usually associated with distress or impairment in important areas of functioning [1]. It then distinguishes a broader category: mental disorders may also be referred to as mental health conditions, which is a broader term covering mental disorders, psychosocial disabilities and other mental states associated with significant distress, impairment in functioning, or risk of self-harm [1]. Three features of that wording deserve attention. The requirement is clinical significance, not severity of feeling. Distress or impairment is usual rather than universal, so a disorder without felt distress is contemplated by the definition itself. And the broader category exists precisely because a great deal of significant suffering does not sit inside the disorder categories at all.

Now watch a line being drawn. NICE's depression guideline needed severities in order to organise its recommendations, and it says so: it defined new episodes as less severe or more severe, explained that less severe depression encompasses subthreshold and mild depression and more severe depression encompasses moderate and severe depression, and stated that thresholds on validated scales were used as an indicator of severity, giving a described scale score of 16 as the dividing point, with scores below defined as less severe and scores at or above as more severe [3]. Read that as a design decision. The committee needed categories to write recommendations about what to offer, it chose a measure and a cut-off to operationalise them, and it published both the choice and its status as an indicator. Nothing about a score of 16 was discovered; a line was placed there, deliberately, for a stated purpose, and the guideline says so plainly.

Why does the placement matter so much? Because the same presentation can be described in more than one way, and the description changes what follows. A person with four weeks of grief-shaped low mood, disturbed sleep and impaired work performance can be described as having a subthreshold depressive episode, or as experiencing distress in the context of a bereavement, and the two descriptions may lead to different routes: one towards a treatment pathway, the other towards support and review. Which description is used will affect a waiting time, a label in a record, and how the person understands themselves. Two structural pressures push in opposite directions. Services under demand pressure have incentives to raise thresholds so that fewer people enter a pathway, and clinicians and the public have incentives to lower them so that more people receive help; both pressures operate on the same boundary, in opposite directions, at different times.

The critique of the categories themselves is mainstream rather than marginal. The National Institute of Mental Health's research framework states that it is not meant to serve as a diagnostic guide and is not intended to replace current diagnostic systems, and explains why a dimensional view is needed: using symptom counts to divide research subjects into two groups of well and ill may obscure important information about the ways in which psychopathology gradually emerges across development [2]. The same point is being made about the boundary from inside: if the phenomena lie on continua, then any cut-off is a decision about where to act rather than a discovery of where nature changes. It is important to hold that alongside the reasons categories exist. Clinicians need shared names to communicate; services need thresholds to allocate scarce capacity; research needs defined groups to be comparable; and people often need a name to make sense of their own experience and to access rights and support. A critique of the boundary is not an argument for abolishing it.

Two failure modes follow directly, and they are the practical content of this lesson. The first is over-inclusion: treating every distress as pathology, which pathologises ordinary responses to loss, adversity and injustice, medicalises what may need practical help, and can make a person's distress worse by telling them something is wrong with them rather than with their circumstances. Lesson 59's material on cultural formulation is the most useful companion here, because cultural variation is one of the places where pathologising happens fastest. The second is under-inclusion: reading the definition strictly and concluding that someone below the threshold is not suffering, or that a person whose distress is not visible in their behaviour is not distressed, which contradicts both the definition's own wording and the reported versus observed discipline of lesson 63. The defensible position is not a firmer line but an explicit one: say what category is being used, for what purpose, and what it excludes.
lessons.example:
Take one fictional presentation and describe it three times, then follow what each description does.

Description one, as a disorder. A 47-year-old woman reports four weeks of persistently low mood, loss of interest in things she normally enjoys, early waking, reduced appetite with weight loss, and difficulty concentrating at work, with no previous episodes. Against the categories in use and an assessment that has excluded obvious physical causes, this meets the shape of a depressive episode of moderate severity. What this description buys: a name she can use, access to a treatment pathway with an evidence base, and a shared shorthand for a team. What it risks: the label hardening into an explanation, and attention to her circumstances and her physical health declining because the category has absorbed the problem.

Description two, as distress in context. The same symptoms in a woman whose husband died eleven weeks ago and who is managing an inheritance dispute, sleeping badly in a house she cannot afford alone. Here the two-description problem appears in its hardest form, because grief of this shape overlaps substantially with the symptom picture, and how the classification should handle that overlap has been argued over repeatedly, including whether a recent bereavement should place a presentation outside the category or inside it with an explanatory note. The existence of that long argument is itself evidence that the boundary is drawn rather than found. What this description buys: attention to the circumstances, an expectation of movement over time, and no premature assumption of a chronic illness. What it risks: the person receiving nothing when she needs help, and grief being treated as a reason to wait rather than a context to work within.

Description three, as a functional problem in a system. The same symptoms again, in a woman whose employer has begun performance management and who describes her low mood as beginning on the day she was told her role was at risk. Here the accurate description may include both a treatable mood state and a real external threat, and a clinician who can only see one of them will be wrong in one direction or the other. What this description buys: recognition that some of what looks like pathology is a response to circumstances, and therefore that some of the help required is practical rather than clinical. What it risks: dismissing a treatable condition as politics.

The exercise is not to find the right description. It is to notice that each description brings a different plan, and that the professional discipline is to say which description is being used, why, and what it leaves out, including the possibility that two are true at once. Notice also the arithmetic of scale that sits behind this: the WHO fact sheet reports that in 2023 nearly 1 in every 7 people around the world were living with a mental disorder, about 1.2 billion people [1], and WHO's own headline of nearly 1 in 7 corresponds to about 14.3 per cent while 1.2 billion against a world population of roughly 8.1 billion is about 14.8 per cent [arithmetic recorded in the handoff]. Working at that scale, reducing the boundary question to a test of whether an individual is really ill is to miss its function entirely.
lessons.question: A fictional service raises its threshold for entry to a treatment pathway and announces that people below the new cut-off are 'not unwell'. Using the definition in this lesson, what is the error in that announcement?
lessons.answer: It converts an administrative decision about who to treat into a claim about who is suffering: the definition requires clinically significant disturbance usually associated with distress or impairment, and a service's threshold determines access rather than whether a person's distress exists.
lessons.distractor: The error is that the threshold excludes people whose disturbance is clinically significant, which the definition forbids, since any clinically significant disturbance is by definition a mental disorder.
lessons.correction: The definition describes a disorder; it does not say that everything below a service's cut-off is not a disorder, and it does not follow from the definition that people above a service's cut-off are disordered either, since services set thresholds using their own criteria. NICE's own wording is instructive: scale thresholds were used as an indicator of severity to organise recommendations, which is a decision about categories for the purpose of organising care. The statement to avoid is the one that confuses the administrative line with the state of the person, in either direction.

depth.definitions: A mental disorder, in WHO's wording, is characterised by a clinically significant disturbance in an individual's cognition, emotional regulation or behaviour, usually associated with distress or impairment in important areas of functioning [1]. Mental health conditions is a broader term covering mental disorders, psychosocial disabilities and other mental states associated with significant distress, impairment in functioning or risk of self-harm [1]. Distress is subjective suffering; impairment is reduced ability to function in important areas such as work, relationships or self-care; the two can occur separately. Clinical significance is the requirement that the disturbance be more than ordinary variation, and it is the least operationalised part of any definition. Subthreshold describes symptoms that fall below a category's requirements. A threshold is the point at which a continuous measure is treated as positive. Nosology is the study of classification. Medicalisation is the process by which ordinary experience comes to be described and managed as illness.
depth.mechanism: Why is the boundary unstable rather than merely imprecise? Four mechanisms are worth separating. First, measurement: the underlying phenomena appear to be dimensional rather than categorical, which is the explicit rationale for NIMH's dimensional framework and its statement that symptom counts dividing people into well and ill groups can obscure how psychopathology emerges gradually [2]. Cutting a dimension produces a line, and the line's location cannot be derived from the dimension itself. Second, purpose: categories are built for different jobs, and a category optimised for recruiting research samples is not the same category needed for deciding who receives a scarce service. Third, incentive: every threshold controls access to something, so the boundary is under continuous pressure from services protecting capacity and from people seeking help, and neither pressure is corrupt in itself. Fourth, culture and history: what counts as a symptom changes across places and decades, which is why lesson 59's cultural formulation and lesson 49's material on language both bear directly on how quickly ordinary distress is converted into a diagnosis. The limits of this account should be stated too. The claim that categories are not natural kinds is itself contested, and the alternative dimensional programmes have not yet produced usable clinical categories; a clinician works with the classification that exists. And the fact that a line is conventional does not mean the phenomena either side of it are unreal, a point that is often lost in arguments on both sides.
depth.secondExample: Consider the boundary question in the opposite direction, from the perspective of a person who receives a diagnosis and finds it useful. A fictional 29-year-old man has spent two years believing that his difficulties are a moral failure: he cannot concentrate, he cannot finish anything, he has been told all his life that he is lazy. When his difficulties are described within a recognised category, three things change. First, his account of his own life alters: what he experienced as a personal defect acquires a name that other people share and that has an evidence base attached to it. Second, his access to adjustments, support and entitlements changes, since many of these are attached to categories. Third, the explanation he can give others changes, which affects how he is treated at work. None of this requires the category to be a natural kind. It requires only that the category be usable and not actively false. Now note the cost in the same case: the label also carries the risk of lowered expectations, of his attention moving from what he can do to what he has, and of his difficulties being treated as a fixed property rather than a current state. The point of setting the two examples side by side is that the boundary's costs and benefits do not fall on abstractions; they fall on people, in directions that depend on what the category makes possible, and the professional obligation is not to have the correct philosophical view but to be explicit about which use of the category is in play.
depth.mistake: The first error is treating the boundary as a discovery, so that a cut-off is spoken about as though it were a fact about human beings rather than a decision taken to organise care; the NICE wording about thresholds used as an indicator is the corrective [3]. The second is the symmetrical error of concluding that because the boundary is conventional, the categories describe nothing, which does not follow and which would leave clinicians without shared names, services without allocation rules and research without comparable groups. The third is confusing the two directions of failure, so that someone who is concerned about medicalising ordinary sadness and someone who is concerned that people are being denied care are treated as opponents, when in practice both concerns operate on the same line and are usually both partly right. The fourth is a wording error with consequences: describing a person's distress as 'not clinically significant' on the basis of a score rather than a person, where lesson 63's discipline about what was observed and reported would have caught it. The fifth, and the one that does most damage in practice, is letting the category displace the formulation: a person is given a name on the first appointment and thereafter is discussed as the name, with the reasons, the circumstances and the trajectory appearing nowhere in the record, which is precisely the collapse of analytical into descriptive work that lesson 51 was about and lesson 70 revisits in writing.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Write three short descriptions of the same fictional presentation, each under 120 words: one as a disorder that meets the shape of a recognised category, one as significant distress in the context of a specific circumstance that does not, and one as both at once. Then add, under each, two lines naming what that description buys and what it risks. Finally, write one sentence stating which description you would use in a note and what would make you change it. Model response and self-review rubric: a strong submission shows that the three descriptions differ in what is claimed about the person, not merely in tone, and each names a specific consequence such as access to a pathway, an expectation about recovery, or a route to practical help. A strong final sentence names an observation that would move you, for instance a change in sleep or function over the following month, rather than naming a repeat of the same score. A weak submission produces three paraphrases of the same description, or asserts that the third description is the correct one, which is the position this lesson argues against. If any of your descriptions implies that a person below a threshold is not suffering, or that a person above one certainly has a disorder, revise it: the lesson's whole point is that a service's threshold and a person's experience are different things.
depth.summary: The line between distress and disorder is drawn rather than found, and the institutions that draw it say so: WHO defines a disorder by clinically significant disturbance usually associated with distress or impairment, adds a broader category for significant suffering that does not fit the disorders, and NICE states that scale thresholds were used as an indicator of severity in defining its categories [1][3]. The boundary is unstable because the phenomena are dimensional, because categories are built for different purposes, because access to scarce resources creates pressure in both directions, and because culture and history move the line. NIMH's own research framework declines to act as a diagnostic guide and warns that symptom counts can obscure gradual emergence [2]. Both failure modes are live: medicalising ordinary distress and denying help to people who fall below a service's cut-off. The workable discipline is not to hold a philosophically settled view of the boundary but to state, at every point, which description is in use, for what purpose, and what it leaves out.

steps: Centre: the findings, separated into reported and observed - four weeks of low mood, early waking, appetite loss, concentration difficulty, function reduced at work.
Description A, disorder of moderate severity: buys a name, a pathway and a shared shorthand; risks the label absorbing the explanation and the circumstances dropping out of the record.

Description B, distress in context following a bereavement and a housing problem: buys attention to circumstances and an expectation of movement; risks the person receiving nothing when help is required.

lessons.title: Substance use assessed without moralising
lessons.explanation:
Assessment of substance use is where clinicians most often stop being clinicians. A person's drinking or drug use attracts judgements that no other part of a history attracts, and those judgements change both what is asked and what is written down. This lesson is about assessment style and record language. It contains no treatment recommendations and no advice about any substance, and nothing here should be used to advise anyone about their own use.

The language argument is the easiest place to start because it is written down. The US National Institute on Drug Abuse publishes a table of terms to use and terms to avoid, with reasons attached [1]. Use person with a substance use disorder rather than addict, user, substance abuser or junkie, because person-first language separates the person from the illness and because the older terms were found to elicit negative associations, punitive attitudes and individual blame [1]. Use person with alcohol use disorder rather than alcoholic or drunk. Use testing positive or negative on a drug screen rather than dirty or clean, since the metaphor of dirt carries a judgement that a laboratory result does not. Use substance use disorder rather than habit or drug addiction, because habit implies that the person is choosing to use or could simply choose to stop, and because describing it as a habit makes the problem appear less serious than it is [1]. Use use for illicit drugs and misuse for prescription medication used other than as prescribed, rather than abuse, since abuse was found to be strongly associated with negative judgement and punishment [1]. Use return to use rather than relapse, and treatment attempt rather than treatment failure [1]. Use medication treatment for opioid use disorder rather than substitution or replacement therapy, because the substitution framing implies that medication merely swaps one dependence for another, which the source describes as a misconception [1]. The handout also recommends using substance use as the general term across substances and referring to severity specifiers such as mild, moderate or severe rather than to colloquial grades [1].

Two things follow from that list. This is not politeness for its own sake: every term on the avoid side encodes a judgement about choice and character, and that judgement is not supported by the evidence the source cites. And the language is asymmetric: the parallel terms used for other illnesses - a person is not described as failing chemotherapy - show how unusual the moral vocabulary of substance use is.

Style follows language. The SAMHSA advisory on motivational approaches describes what practitioners actually do: the four interwoven processes are partnership, acceptance, compassion and evocation, in which the provider influences gently but the person drives the conversation, and reflective listening, expressing empathy, is described as fundamental to person-centred counselling and to the approach as a whole [2]. The advisory also reports that providers' expressions of empathy are predictive of improved substance use outcomes, citing a study of therapist empathy and alcohol outcomes, and that skilled practitioners offer reflections more often than they ask questions [2]. Treat the second of those as evidence about therapeutic style in a treatment context rather than as a conversation rule for an assessment, and treat the outcome claim as reported in that source rather than as a general law.

Now the assessment content, which is where clinicians who have absorbed the language message often under-invest. The questions that matter are about pattern and function: what the substance does for this person, at what times, in what contexts, what it makes better, what it costs, what the person has tried before and what happened, and what the person wants now. Function is the specific term for the last of these: every substance that is used recurrently is doing something in a person's life, whether that is sleep, pain, anxiety, social participation or the avoidance of something unbearable, and a plan that ignores the function will fail because the function remains uncovered. Consequences then become part of the same inquiry rather than a rhetorical weapon: what has changed as a result, financially, physically, relationally, legally, and what does the person themselves count as a cost. Note the difference in the record between 'reports drinking a bottle of spirits most evenings, says it helps him sleep, has had two falls in the last month and had not connected them' and 'denies any problem'. The first is an assessment; the second is a verdict, and it is also inaccurate, because the person's own description has disappeared.

The last element is sequencing, and here a guideline observation is genuinely useful because it is easy to get backwards. NICE's alcohol guideline states that for service users whose comorbid mental health problems do not significantly improve after abstinence from alcohol, typically after three to four weeks, specific treatment for the comorbid problem should be considered [3]. Read that as an observation about assessment order rather than a clinical instruction: the guideline acknowledges that anxiety, low mood, poor sleep and irritability can be consequences of use and can also be pre-existing conditions, and it explicitly builds in a period during which the picture is allowed to clarify. This is the same principle as lesson 54's two-way street between physical illness and mental state, applied to substances, and it has a direct bearing on interviewing: a clinician who concludes on day one that the problem is depression and the drinking is secondary has closed the question the guideline asks to remain open.

One final point about thoroughness, because non-judgemental is not the same as incurious. A style that avoids moralising is compatible with asking detailed questions about quantity, frequency, timing, withdrawal symptoms and physical consequences, and a clinician who skips those questions to avoid seeming censorious has confused kindness with neglect. Withdrawal from a substance is a medical matter with recognised risks managed by clinicians, and this course does not cover it; the point here is that assessment must include whether it has occurred and what was observed, because the answer changes what the picture means.
lessons.example:
A fictional 39-year-old man attends an emergency department after a fall at home. Two versions of the relevant part of the assessment follow.

Version one. The clinician records: 'patient smelled of alcohol, denies problem drinking, poor insight, habitual drinker, unhelpful and evasive about how much he drinks, likely alcohol dependence'. Notice what has happened. The clinical information is minimal and the moral material is abundant. 'Denies problem drinking' records a category the man never claimed to have and does not say what he was asked or what he said. 'Poor insight' is doing work that belongs to specific questions about what he thinks has happened. 'Habitual' and 'likely dependent' are inferences built on a smell and a fall. 'Unhelpful and evasive' converts a probable response to a judgemental question into a trait. An accurate and more useful version of the same 90 seconds would look quite different.

Version two. The clinician asks what happened and stays with it: 'Drinks most evenings after his shift, usually four to six cans; describes it as the only thing that stops him sleeping badly, which he dates to his separation two years ago. Slept badly when he stopped for a week in March; described sweating and shaking and said he was "all over the place" for three days. Two falls in the last month, both in the evening; he had not connected them. Says "I know it's not helping but I don't know what else to do at nine o'clock." Says he does not want to stop completely; wants to sleep.' Now notice what the note contains: a pattern with quantities, a function, a context, a withdrawal history in the person's own words, consequences the person had not connected, and the person's own goal. There is no verdict in it at all, and it says more about what to do next than version one, even though it makes no recommendation.

The contrast extends to spoken style. In version one the questions were probably closed and accusatory - how much do you drink, do you think that's wise, are you ready to admit - and the answers came back accordingly. In version two the clinician's opening question was directive and about circumstances rather than about quantity: what does the evening look like for you? The function question then did the work that a moralising question cannot do, which is to identify what the drinking is holding together. Note also what did not happen in version two: the clinician did not tell the man that his drinking was fine, did not agree that he could not stop, and did not omit the falls. Non-judgemental questioning produced more of the information that a judgemental approach was trying to obtain, and interestingly the man's own remark - I don't know what else to do at nine o'clock - is the closest thing in the whole record to a statement of need, and it only appears in the version where he was not being graded.
lessons.question: A fictional clinician is asked why 'reports smoking heroin' should be preferred to 'is a drug abuser' in a note. What is the best answer?
lessons.answer: The first records what the person says and separates them from the behaviour, while the second names the person as the problem and carries the negative judgement and punitive associations that the language guidance documents for the word abuse.
lessons.distractor: The first is preferred because it is vaguer and therefore safer against complaints, while the second records a definite clinical fact about the person's dependence.
lessons.correction: The distinction is not between vagueness and certainty, and 'drug abuser' is not a clinical fact: it is a description of the person rather than of the behaviour, and the published guidance specifically recommends using use or misuse in place of abuse because the latter has been found to be strongly associated with negative judgement and punishment. Precision is available in other directions, for example by recording the substance, the pattern, the function, the consequences and what the person says about their own use, all of which are more informative than the label that was removed.

depth.definitions: Substance use is consumption of a substance, including alcohol and prescribed medication used other than as prescribed; use and misuse are preferred to the word abuse in the published language guidance [1]. A substance use disorder is the clinical category, with severity specifiers such as mild, moderate or severe in the guidance's own framing [1]. Return to use replaces relapse, and treatment attempt replaces treatment failure, according to the same source [1]. Person-first language places the person before the condition, as in person with a substance use disorder [1]. Function of use names what the substance does in the person's life at a particular time, such as sleep onset, pain relief, anxiety reduction or social participation. Withdrawal is the physiological and psychological change that occurs when use of a substance on which the person is dependent is reduced or stopped, and it is a medical matter managed by clinicians. Motivational style, in the advisory's framing, rests on partnership, acceptance, compassion and evocation, with reflective listening described as fundamental [2].
depth.mechanism: Why does moralising reduce the quality of an assessment? Four connected mechanisms. The first is disclosure: what a person will say depends on how they expect to be judged, and the research summarised in lesson 64 on interpreters showed the same effect in a different domain, where the identity of the listener changed how much sensitive material was disclosed. The second is question design: moralising tends to travel with closed and leading questions such as do you think that is wise, which produce compliance or defensiveness rather than information. The third is record drift: once the note contains a verdict, later readers stop asking questions that the verdict appears to have answered, so a judgement in the file suppresses inquiry. The fourth is the mechanism behind the language guidance itself, which is not aesthetic: terms such as abuse and addict were found to carry negative associations and to elicit punitive attitudes, so the words change how the person is treated by the next clinician, and in some systems by insurers and courts [1]. Now the reason function matters as a mechanism rather than a question type. If the substance is holding something in place, then assessing only quantity and consequence describes the problem without describing the system, and any plan formed on that assessment leaves the function uncovered. The limit should be stated clearly: the evidence for specific language effects is consensus guidance and survey research rather than trials of outcomes, and the empathy findings the advisory cites concern therapy rather than assessment interviews, so the case for non-moralising assessment rests on the quality of information obtained and on the ethics of how a person is described, not on a demonstrated outcome effect in an assessment setting.
depth.secondExample: Consider a fictional 24-year-old woman referred by her employer after two unexplained absences, who is using stimulants on weekends. The moralising version of this assessment is easy to anticipate: it produces a note about irresponsible behaviour and a recommendation about adherence, and it misses what is happening. Suppose the function questions reveal that the weekend use began after she started a night-shift rota, that it is used to stay awake for a second job on Saturdays and to feel socially capable on Sundays, and that she is frightened of becoming like a parent whose use she grew up with, which is why she has told nobody and why she arrived at the appointment thirty minutes early. Now the picture has structure: a financial requirement, a sleep problem created by shift work, a social function, and a fear that is itself an obstacle to disclosure. None of that appears in the moralising version, and all of it changes what a clinician can usefully discuss. Notice too how the person's own goal appears here, since she has not been asked whether she wants to stop: she says she wants to be able to sleep on Saturday nights without using anything. A final observation about this example: the reason the assessment worked is not that the clinician avoided the word abuse, though that mattered, but that the clinician asked about pattern, context and function, which are questions a moralising clinician tends not to ask because the verdict feels already established.
depth.mistake: The first error is the verdict in the record: denies any problem, poor insight, non-compliant, evasive. These are conclusions about a person's character written in the grammar of findings, and the correct repair is to record what was asked, what was said and what was observed. The second is treating a denial as a lie rather than as information about the question, which is lesson 62's point applied to a context where the pressure to disbelieve is strongest. The third is abandoning thoroughness in the name of kindness: a clinician who does not ask about quantities, timing, withdrawal, physical consequences or prior attempts has not been gentle, only uninformed, and has left the person's own safety questions unexamined. The fourth is using the language guidance mechanically, so that a note becomes euphemistic; person-first language is about separating the person from the condition, not about avoiding the substance's name. The fifth is deciding the order of the clinical picture on day one, either by treating the drinking as the whole problem and dismissing the low mood, or by treating the mood as primary and never examining the use; the guideline's own three to four week observation period exists because the direction cannot be settled in advance [3]. The sixth, and the one most likely to cause harm, is a style that avoids moralising in the consulting room and then reverts to it in the referral letter, where the person cannot answer back.
depth.application: Non-blocking task in three parts. First, rewrite these three phrases into assessment language, then add the exact question you would have asked to obtain each: 'denies problem drinking'; 'known drug user, chaotic'; 'poor compliance with appointments'. Second, write five questions about a fictional person's substance use that between them cover pattern, function, context, consequences and the person's own goal, none of which contains a judgement about the behaviour. Third, write a 100-word note paragraph for the same fictional person that uses person-first language, includes the function of the use and one thing the person said in their own words, and contains no verdict. Model response and self-review rubric: a strong rewrite of 'denies problem drinking' names what was asked - for example whether the person drinks and what it does for them - and reports the answer in their terms, with quantity and timing if given. A strong question set contains at least one question about the times of day or situations in which use occurs, and at least one question about what the person wants, which is the question most often absent. A weak submission contains any of the words addict, abuser, clean, dirty, habit or failure as descriptions of the person, or contains a sentence that grades the person's honesty. If your note has no quotation from the person in it, revise: an assessment in which the person's own words do not appear is a description of a category, not of a person.
depth.summary: Assessing substance use without moralising is a technical skill with a published vocabulary and a defined question set. The language guidance is explicit about which terms encode judgement and why, from abuse and addict to clean and dirty to relapse and treatment failure [1]. The questioning style rests on partnership, acceptance, compassion and evocation, with reflective listening at its centre and empathy reported as predictive of outcomes in treatment studies [2]. The content is pattern, function, context, consequences, prior attempts and the person's own goal, and function is the element that a moralising assessment almost always loses. Non-judgemental does not mean incurious: quantities, timing, withdrawal and physical consequences remain part of a complete assessment, and withdrawal in particular changes what the picture means. Sequencing is a live question rather than a settled one, which is why the guideline builds in a period during which comorbid symptoms are allowed to clarify before they are treated as a separate problem [3]. What the whole approach obtains is the thing the moralising version was trying to force: a person's account of their own use, including what it is holding in place.

visual.title: Two notes on the same 90 seconds: verdict versus assessment
visual.description: A page split vertically. Left side, headed 'verdict', lists moral descriptors with no question and no quotation attached. Right side, headed 'assessment', lists pattern, function, context, consequences and the person's own words. Arrows cross from each left-hand item to the question on the right side that would have produced information instead.
steps: Left: 'denies problem drinking' - arrow to right: what was asked, and what did the person say about their drinking?
Left: 'habitual drinker' - arrow to right: pattern - which days, what quantity, at what time of day.
Left: 'unhelpful and evasive' - arrow to right: what was observed in the exchange, and what was the person's own stated goal?
Right: function - what the drinking does for the person, in their account, such as stopping the mind at night.
Right: context and consequences - shift work, relationship change, two falls, whether the person connected them.
Right: the person's words in quotation marks, including any statement of what they want, which is the line most often missing from a verdict-style note.
Rule box: person-first language throughout; no grading of the person's honesty; unknown recorded as unknown.

lessons.title: Capstone: the assessment write-up, separating findings, formulation and plan - with uncertainty documented
lessons.explanation:
Everything in this level ends in a document. The interview produced material, the observation produced material, the instruments produced numbers, the interpreter mediated some of it, and now somebody has to write it down in a way that a stranger can use and that the person themselves would recognise. This capstone is about that document: its three layers, the standards that govern it, and the discipline of writing uncertainty rather than concealing it. It remains education about clinical method, not a template for diagnosing or treating anyone.

The first layer is findings. Findings are what was reported, what was observed and what was measured, each marked as such. The mental status examination's own internal convention is the model: mood recorded in the person's words and quoted, affect recorded as the clinician's interpretation of observed expression, and neutrality maintained where the two do not line up (the convention set out in lesson 63, from the StatPearls mental status examination entry). Findings include the negative material, but only where it was actually examined: 'no tremor observed' is a finding, while 'no abnormalities' in a section nobody assessed is a gap dressed as a result. Findings also include the conditions under which they were obtained, because those conditions change what the finding means: a self-report given in an emergency department at two in the morning, through an interpreter, twelve hours into withdrawal, or in front of a family member, is a different measurement from the same words spoken in a planned appointment.

The second layer is the formulation. It is not a summary with better adjectives. Gareth Owen's review puts the distinction sharply, describing a summary as descriptive and a formulation as analytical and evaluative, and noting that two experts assessing the same patient may produce similar-looking summaries but different formulations [1]. The 4P grid that he traces - predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating and protective factors across biological, psychological and social domains - gives the discipline that keeps a formulation from becoming a story: each proposed causal factor needs some basis for its causal role, each proposed change needs a reason to believe it would modify that factor, and some factors will be marked as unknown or not currently modifiable [1]. A formulation that could not be wrong is not a formulation; it is a conviction.

The third layer is the plan. A plan answers four questions in the document: what will happen, who will do it, by when, and what would cause it to change. The last of those is the one most often omitted and the one that makes the plan testable. A plan that says the person will be reviewed in four weeks, with a named contact in the meantime, that states which observation would trigger earlier contact, and that records the person's own stated priorities, has been written by somebody who expects to be accountable to it. A plan that says 'continue current management, review as needed' has recorded that a decision was made and nothing about what it was.

On the standards that govern the document, the General Medical Council's guidance sets out both the requirement and the content. Records must be clear, accurate, contemporaneous and legible, and taking a proportionate approach to detail, records should usually include relevant clinical findings, drugs, investigations or treatments proposed, provided or prescribed, the information shared with patients, concerns or preferences expressed by the patient that might be relevant to their ongoing care and whether these were addressed, information about any reasonable adjustments and communication support preferences, decisions made and actions agreed including decisions to take no action, and when or whether those decisions should be reviewed, and who is creating the record and when [2]. Read that list carefully, because three of its items are routinely dropped. Preferences expressed and whether they were addressed: a person's own stated priority is clinical information. Decisions to take no action: the most common decision in psychiatry, and the one most often left out, which makes it invisible to the next reviewer. And a review date: the sentence that converts a plan from an assertion into a commitment. The same guidance requires records containing personal information to be kept securely and in line with data protection law, which is a reminder that the document is not the clinician's private reasoning space [2]. Access caveat: the GMC's site refused direct automated requests during the preparation of this lesson, so its content was read through an extraction tool and a search index that returned the same wording from the Council's own pages; a reader should confirm the wording in a browser.

Now the part that makes the document honest: declared uncertainty. Every statement in a write-up occupies one of four positions - reported, observed, measured or inferred - and each should be legible as itself. Beyond marking provenance, three specific practices carry most of the weight. Name what would change the conclusion, in a form that could be checked: 'if the sleep pattern does not change over the next month, the sleep-driven account of his low mood will need revisiting' is checkable; 'if he deteriorates, reconsider' is not. Name the disagreement rather than resolving it: where the person disputes the formulation, the record should say so and say what they offered instead, because a reader who inherits only the clinician's version cannot see the reasoning that is at stake. And name absence: what could not be assessed in this encounter, and when it will be. Where risk is part of the picture, the guidance requires a risk formulation as part of every psychosocial assessment, which is a written account of needs, of situations that would raise risk and of planned actions rather than a category or a number [3].

Two failure modes are worth naming, because both are common and both look professional. The first is the fluent document that decides nothing: pleasant prose, no named findings, no factor marked unknown, no review date, and no sentence a reader could contradict. It is often produced by clinicians who are being careful, and it fails the person because nothing in it can be acted on or contested. The second is the opposite: a document so confident that it forecloses the next assessment. Both failures share a cause, which is that writing a formulation requires taking a position, and taking a position feels riskier than describing. The remedy is not caution but explicitness: a position that states its basis, its limits and its review date is safer than a description that appears to have no author.
lessons.example:
Below is a fictional write-up of a first assessment, once as a fluent and uninformative document and once in three layers. The person is a 21-year-old student referred by his tutor after a term of falling grades and missed seminars.

Version one, fluent and empty. 'Mr B attended for assessment. He presented as a pleasant young man who engaged well. There were some difficulties with motivation and low mood, likely related to the pressures of his course. No concerns regarding risk were identified. He would benefit from support and a review in due course.' Notice what a reader cannot do with this. There is no account of what he said, so nobody can tell what the difficulties consist of. 'Some difficulties' has no duration, frequency or functional impact. 'Likely related to the pressures of his course' is a causal claim with no basis and, worse, it is plausible, which is what makes it dangerous, since it will be accepted without argument. 'No concerns regarding risk were identified' implies a risk inquiry that is not described and may not have happened. 'Review in due course' contains no review. The document reads as competent because the sentences are grammatical and the tone is calm, which is exactly the property that makes it hard to challenge.

Version two, three layers. Findings. 'Reported: sleeps 3-4 hours, falling asleep around 04:00 and waking at 11:00 or later most days; has missed 11 of 20 seminars this term; says "I can't make myself care about anything and then I panic about the consequences"; describes two weeks in December when he "was fine, actually better than fine" and slept very little without feeling tired; says he has not used any substances since starting university except alcohol at weekends; says he has not told his parents. Observed: appeared older than his stated age in presentation but well groomed; speech normal in rate, occasionally pressured when describing the December period; eye contact maintained; no unusual perceptual experiences reported on direct questioning, with the person's own terms for the experiences recorded. Measured: not administered. Unknown: family history, childhood development, any previous episodes, current risk to himself, and the extent of alcohol use, none of which were covered in this 40-minute appointment.'

Formulation. 'Load-bearing: a two-week period of reduced need for sleep with elevated energy and pressured speech in December, followed by a return of severe sleep disruption and impaired function. This pattern is the reason the current low mood is not being treated as the primary problem, because a period of diminished need for sleep with increased activity is not typical of depression alone and is the observation that most changes the ordering of the questions. Also load-bearing: the term's academic collapse, which is real, consequential and not by itself an explanation for the sleep pattern. Marked as plausible but unevidenced: that the December period was triggered by the end-of-term workload. Marked unknown: whether there has been any earlier episode, which the family history and developmental history would address, and whether alcohol use has any bearing. Not currently modifiable: examination deadlines, which fall within the next three weeks and which shape what can be attempted.'

Plan. 'A further appointment in five days, of an hour, covering developmental and family history, previous episodes, a full assessment of alcohol use, and a direct discussion of risk to himself, which will be asked about plainly at the start rather than left to the end. A named contact within the team for the interval. The person's own stated priority is recorded as wanting to stop "losing the term" rather than to discuss the December period, and this will be addressed first in the next appointment because his engagement depends on it. The plan would change if he reports a sustained pattern of unusually reduced need for sleep with high activity in the next week, if he discloses escalating alcohol use, or if any risk to himself emerges in the next appointment; in those cases an earlier review and a wider assessment would follow.'

Compare the two. The second is longer and says less about what the person is like; it makes no pronouncement about his character, and it contains three explicit unknowns, one unevidenced claim, an unmodifiable factor and a falsifiable statement of what would change the plan. It also records that a person's stated priority will be addressed first, which is the item most often dropped from a real document. Nothing in it is a diagnosis, and nothing in it is advice to the reader; it is an example of the separation this level has been teaching.
lessons.question: A fictional junior clinician writes a formulation that accounts for everything in the assessment, explains each finding and cannot be contradicted by any observation in the record. What is the methodological problem?
lessons.answer: A formulation that no possible observation could contradict is unfalsifiable, which makes it a conviction rather than an analysis: it should name which factor is load-bearing, mark the unevidenced and unknown ones, and state what would change it.
lessons.distractor: The problem is that a formulation should not attempt to account for observed findings at all, because only the person's own account may be used in a formulation.
lessons.correction: A formulation is analytical and evaluative rather than descriptive, which is exactly why it may take a position on the observed material; what it may not do is take a position that could not be shown to be wrong. The corrective is the discipline taught with the four Ps: each proposed causal factor needs a basis for its causal role, each proposed action needs a reason to think it modifies that factor, and some entries will be marked unknown or not modifiable. The clinician should add the sentence that makes the argument testable, naming an observation that would force a revision, and then set a review date.

depth.definitions: Findings are what was reported, observed and measured, marked as such. A summary is descriptive; a formulation is analytical and evaluative, and two clinicians with identical notes may write different formulations [1]. Predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating and protective factors are the four temporal categories that structure a formulation, applied across biological, psychological and social domains [1]. A risk formulation is a documented account of needs, of situations in which risk would increase and of planned actions, required as part of every psychosocial assessment [3]. Declared provenance is the marking of each statement as reported, observed, measured or inferred. A review date is the date by which the plan will be reconsidered, and it is part of the record rather than an administrative nicety [2]. Contemporaneous means made at the time of the events or as soon as possible afterwards [2].
depth.mechanism: Why does the three-layer structure matter more than the writing style? Because each layer does a different job for a different reader. Findings let a reader check the reasoning, since without them a formulation cannot be audited and a diagnosis cannot be revisited. Formulation lets a reader see why this plan and not another, and it is where the clinician's own position is exposed to criticism; the reason it must be analytical rather than descriptive is that a description cannot be argued with [1]. The plan lets a reader act, which requires a who, a when and a trigger for change. Uncertainty is not a fourth layer but a property of the first three: the same sentence can be a finding with a known basis, a finding with an unknown basis, or an inference, and the difference is legibility rather than honesty in the abstract. The mechanism by which documentation improves care is mostly indirect and should be stated as such: it supports continuity between professionals, it makes the reasoning available to the person and to review processes, and it forces the writer to decide what they actually think. Two limits are worth naming. First, a good document does not make the assessment correct: a well-written formulation of a mistaken inference is still a mistaken inference, and writing style can give bad reasoning an appearance of rigour. Second, written uncertainty is not universally welcomed, and in systems where a hedge is read as indecision, the discipline of stating what would change the conclusion is both more defensible and more useful than either false precision or vague caution.
depth.secondExample: Now consider the same three layers written for a person who disputes the account, which is where the writing discipline is most severely tested. A fictional 48-year-old woman with a long history of contact with services says in the appointment that the diagnosis she carries is wrong, that she has never had the condition described in her notes, and that the notes have done her harm. A clinician writing a summary that silently resolves the disagreement will produce a document that is coherent and unfair: it will state the diagnosis as fact, describe her objections as a symptom, and leave her with no way to see that she was heard. Written in three layers, the same appointment produces something different. Findings: what she said, in her words, including the claim that the notes have harmed her; what was observed, including the fact that she produced a dated list of her own and was able to trace each incident; what was measured and what was not. Formulation: the current formulation, marked as the clinician's own position, with the specific observations that support it and the fact stated explicitly that she disputes it, together with the account she offers; and a note of what would move the position, for example access to the earlier records that she has asked for. Plan: what will happen next, including what she asked for and whether it was addressed, and a review date. The document now contains both accounts, keeps the clinician's reasoning visible, and records that a request was made. This is the practical meaning of the GMC's requirement that records include concerns or preferences expressed by the patient that might be relevant to their ongoing care and whether these were addressed, and decisions made and actions agreed including decisions to take no action [2]. Note what has not happened: the clinician has not abandoned their formulation, and has not adopted hers. Both are on the page, and a third reader can weigh them.
depth.mistake: The first error is the fluent empty document, in which grammatical calm substitutes for content and every paragraph is unfalsifiable; its diagnostic signature is the absence of any sentence a reader could contradict, and its remedy is to require one named observation that would change the conclusion. The second is the disguise of inference as finding, for example writing that a person was avoidant or minimising or lacks insight, which converts a judgement into something later readers will treat as data. The third is the missing plan detail: no named person, no date, no trigger, which makes the document historical rather than operational. The fourth is omitting the person's own preferences and their disagreement, which the standards require to be recorded with a note of whether they were addressed [2], and which practice suggests is one of the most commonly dropped items. The fifth is the false certainty of a risk statement: a category or a reassurance, where the guidance asks for a formulation naming needs, triggers and actions [3]. The sixth is a specific and under-noticed failure: recording what was found and not what was absent, so a later reader cannot tell whether a question was asked and answered negatively or never asked at all. The seventh is verbosity as concealment: a document long enough that nobody reads to the end is a document in which an omission is unlikely to be discovered.
depth.application: Non-blocking capstone task. Using a fictional person of your own devising, write an assessment document of no more than 450 words with three explicitly headed layers. Findings: separate reported, observed, measured and unknown, using quotation for the person's own words and marking the conditions under which the information was obtained. Formulation: name the load-bearing factor, mark at least one entry as plausible but unevidenced, one as unknown and one as not currently modifiable, and state who the person's account differs from yours if it does. Plan: what will happen, who will do it, by when, what the person asked for and whether it was addressed, and one checkable statement of what would change the plan. Model response and self-review rubric: a strong document contains at least one explicit unknown, at least one statement attributed to the person in their own words, a review date, and a falsifiable sentence of the form 'if X is observed, then Y will be reconsidered'. A strong formulation does not list a diagnosis as a cause. Weak documents read smoothly and contain none of these; a useful diagnostic test is to hunt for the sentence that could be contradicted, and if there is none, rewrite until there is one. A submission that describes the fictional person only in adjectives, with no reported material and no unknowns, should be rewritten before submission: it is the fluent empty document this lesson is about, and it is a common and consequential professional failure.
depth.summary: The assessment write-up is the last and most durable product of everything this level teaches. Findings separate reported, observed, measured and unknown material, and they say how and where they were obtained. Formulation is analytical and evaluative rather than descriptive, disciplined by the four Ps and by the requirement that each causal claim has a basis and each proposed change a reason, with unknown and unmodifiable factors marked as such [1]. Plan names what happens, who does it, by when, what the person asked for and whether it was addressed, and what would change the plan, all of which the standards require in substance [2]. Uncertainty is a property that runs through all three layers: provenance, explicit unknowns, stated disagreement and a checkable revision condition. Risk, where it arises, is written as a formulation of needs, triggers and actions rather than a category or a number [3]. The two failures to avoid are the fluent document that decides nothing and the confident document that forecloses the next assessment, and both are avoided by the same move: take a position, show its basis, show its limits, and date its review.

The article is a review with an argument of its own about the value of formulation, so read it as a position, and notice that it is also honest about the criticism the concept has attracted.
