This course does not teach risk assessment and nothing here should be used to judge anyone's safety.

visual.title: The three-layer document with a provenance margin
visual.description: A single page divided into three headed bands - findings, formulation, plan - with a narrow margin column running down the left side in which each paragraph is tagged R (reported), O (observed), M (measured), I (inferred) or U (unknown). A boxed line at the foot of the page holds the revision condition and the review date, and a second box lists the person's own stated preferences and whether they were addressed.
steps: Band one, findings: reported material quoted verbatim; observed material in concrete detail; measured material with the instrument named and the number reported as a number, not as a conclusion; unknown material named as unknown.
Margin tags: every paragraph carries R, O, M, I or U so that provenance survives editing.

Band two, formulation: load-bearing factor named first; each further entry marked with its basis, including at least one plausible-but-unevidenced, one unknown and one not-currently-modifiable item; the person's differing account recorded where it exists.
Band three, plan: what will happen, who will do it, by when, what would change it, and the person's stated priority with a note of whether it was addressed.
Foot box one: the revision condition, written so that it could be checked - 'if X is observed, Y will be reconsidered'.
Foot box two: review date, the name of the person writing the record and the date it was written, and any decision to take no action recorded explicitly.

questions.prompt: A fictional crisis service introduces a short self-report questionnaire scored by total, with the total sorted into low, medium and high bands, and the band attached to the person's record and used to decide who is seen first. The service's rationale is that staff are overloaded and the bands are objective. Using this level's material, what is the strongest criticism?
questions.answer: The band replaces a written formulation of needs, triggers and planned actions with a number, which the guideline on self-harm specifically warns against for prediction and stratification, and which also removes the material a clinician actually needs in order to act.
questions.distractor: The criticism is that total scores from self-report questionnaires are always invalid, because only clinician-rated instruments may be used in an urgent assessment.
questions.correction: The objection is not to measurement as such: a validated measure can be a legitimate part of an assessment and can be used to inform and evaluate care. What the guidance rejects is using a tool to predict who will repeat self-harm or to sort people into risk categories, on the grounds that such instruments are not able to do that, and a band that follows a person through their record also implies a stable property where the assessment is of a situation. The repair is to keep whatever measure the service values as one input, and to require instead the written account the guidance asks for: needs, the situations that would raise risk, and planned actions, developed with the person.

questions.prompt: A fictional clinician asks a person in distress whether they are going to 'do anything silly', receives a no, and records 'no suicidal ideation, low risk'. Two weeks later the person discloses that they had been thinking about ending their life throughout that appointment. What went wrong, in this level's terms?
questions.answer: The question was euphemistic and indirect, so the answer it produced does not establish what the record claims; the plain question about suicide was not asked, the record converted the person's response into a risk verdict, and neither the person's words nor the limits of the inquiry were documented.
questions.distractor: Nothing procedural went wrong: a person who does not disclose thoughts of suicide at a direct appointment cannot be assessed for them, since risk interviewing depends on voluntary disclosure.
questions.correction: Disclosure depends heavily on how the question is asked and on the record being an account of what was asked rather than a verdict, and indirect phrasing such as 'anything silly' invites a denial by implying what the answer should be. The plain question is the one to ask, and the recommended framing is available in the public health guidance cited in lesson 66. Two repairs belong in the note: state the question that was asked and the person's answer in their own words, and state plainly what was not assessed, since a conclusion of low risk that was never examined is the failure this lesson calls treating a verdict as a finding.

questions.prompt: A fictional team is discussing a man who says he will not take the medication offered because he believes it caused his previous admission. One member of the team says this proves he lacks insight and that the team should proceed on the basis of what is best for him. Using this level's material, what is wrong with that move?
questions.answer: It converts a dispute about explanation and a disagreement about treatment into a global rating of insight and then treats that rating as if it settled the separate legal question of whether he can decide for himself.
questions.distractor: It is wrong because a person who refuses a treatment offered by a team cannot be judged to lack insight, since insight is defined as agreement with the clinical team's view.
questions.correction: Insight is disputed and multidimensional, its instruments disagree, and its published definitions involve awareness of change and the ability to consider being mistaken rather than agreement with a team; the evidence linking poor insight to poorer adherence is also correlational and cannot be applied to an individual's decision. More importantly, insight is not capacity: a person can dispute a formulation and still understand, retain, weigh and communicate a decision about a specific treatment, which is the test that governs whether the decision must be respected, and a clinical team's judgement about best interests does not displace it.

questions.prompt: A fictional note about a 31-year-old woman reads: 'Known drug user, chaotic lifestyle, denies problem use, poor compliance with appointments, unlikely to engage. Habitual use of multiple substances.' Using this level's material, what is the main problem?
questions.answer: The note records verdicts about the person rather than an assessment of the use: the substances, pattern, timing, function, context, consequences and the person's own goal are all missing, and the language used carries the judgements the published guidance recommends avoiding.
questions.distractor: The note is too detailed about matters that are not clinically relevant, and the correct approach is to record only whether the person is using substances and whether they wish to stop.
questions.correction: Thoroughness in this area is not optional: quantity, pattern, timing, withdrawal and physical consequences all change what the picture means, and the person's own goal is the single most useful line a note can contain. What should be removed is the moral vocabulary - the guidance recommends person-first terms, use or misuse rather than abuse, and return to use rather than relapse - and what should be added is the function of the use. 'Denies problem use' records a category the person never claimed and does not say what was asked or answered, which is the same substitution of a verdict for a finding that lessons 63 and 70 address.

questions.prompt: Read this fictional handover paragraph: 'Ms C has a long history of emotional instability and recurrent crises. She was admitted last night after an argument with her partner. She is well known to the team and always difficult to engage. Current plan: continue current management, review as needed.' Which single criticism best captures what is missing, in this level's terms?
questions.answer: It is descriptive rather than analytical and contains nothing checkable: no reported or observed findings distinguish the admission, no load-bearing factor is named, no trigger for earlier review is stated, and a decision to take no action beyond routine review is not recorded as a decision.
questions.distractor: It is too brief, and the remedy is a longer narrative account of Ms C's previous admissions so that the next team has more background.
questions.correction: Length is not the problem; length is often the mechanism by which an omission goes undiscovered. The paragraph fails at the layer of formulation, which the review cited in lesson 70 defines as analytical and evaluative, requiring each proposed causal factor to have a basis for its causal role; and it fails at the layer of plan, which should name what happens, who does it, by when and what would change it. The phrase 'always difficult to engage' also puts a judgement in the grammar of an observation, and recording 'review as needed' omits both the review date and any decision to take no further action, which the record-keeping guidance requires to be stated explicitly.

questions.prompt: A fictional psychiatrist is asked to assess a man on a busy ward at 1 a.m., thirty-six hours after admission, whose speech is rapid and who keeps returning to the same grievance. She has twenty minutes. Which approach follows this level's teaching about interview structure and question form?
questions.answer: Open the interview with a brief unpressured question and let him speak without interruption, then narrow to the specific areas with closed questions, and record what was said and the conditions under which it was obtained.
questions.distractor: Because of the time limit, the correct approach is to complete a structured question list first so that the twenty minutes produce comparable data, and to leave any open questioning to a later appointment.
questions.correction: Order matters for a specific reason: a clinician who has not heard the person's own account cannot know which focused questions are the relevant ones in this case, so starting with a checklist on a twenty-minute clock produces coverage without content and, as the interview research shows, risks narrower and more discrepant results. The 1 a.m. condition is not a reason to skip the narrative; it is a finding that belongs in the record, because material gathered thirty-six hours into an admission at one in the morning means something different from the same words spoken in a planned appointment.

questions.prompt: A fictional note reads: 'Appeared agitated and guarded. Denied any problems at home. Reported that his wife was "fine about everything". Affect was flat and inappropriate.' Which statement best applies this level's discipline about reported and observed material?
questions.answer: Agitation and flat affect are observations and belong as observed, but the two reported items are mis-stated: what he said about home and his wife's views is a report, and a negative report is not evidence about the marriage, while the judgement that the affect was inappropriate conflates an observation with a conclusion about what it should have been.
questions.distractor: The note is correctly written, because a clinician's overall impression of agitation and guardedness summarises both what the person said and what was seen, and separating the two would make the record less usable.
questions.correction: Two distinct corrections are needed. First, a denial is a report about the interview: what the person was asked and what he said should be recorded, and the inference that all is well at home is not licensed by it, which is the lesson-62 error of treating silence and negation as evidence. Second, 'inappropriate' asserts a norm for an observation; the observable content is that the affect did not vary as the person described distressing events, which is checkable, whereas 'inappropriate' is not. Where the observation is genuinely a clinician's interpretation, the mental status examination's own convention is to mark it as such, which is how mood recorded in the person's words and affect recorded as the clinician's impression are kept apart.

questions.prompt: A fictional service administers a self-report symptom questionnaire to a woman with limited English, and an interpreter who knows her family translates the items aloud, explaining them in his own words. The score is recorded and used in the formulation. What is the main problem?
questions.answer: The instrument's score is not the instrument's score: sight translation by somebody known to the person, without pre-briefing or translation of the wording, produces a result whose validity is unknown, so it should be reported as an informal verbal administration with that limitation stated rather than as a measured finding.
questions.distractor: The problem is that interpreters should never be used for a clinical assessment of any kind, because interpretation distorts the person's meaning beyond recovery.
questions.correction: Interpreters are required for good assessment, and the guidance cited in lesson 64 goes further than that, saying the interpreter should be independent of the person's family and social circle and that the person should be offered a choice about the interpreter's characteristics. What the guidelines advise for instruments is specific: a formally translated version is preferred, sight translation of a questionnaire is discouraged, and where an informal translation has been used this should be documented along with the caution that the score may not be valid. There is a second issue in the scenario: the person's level of English must be assessed for the task at hand rather than assumed from conversational fluency, which is lesson 64's point about proficiency varying with subject matter and clinical state.

questions.prompt: A fictional team meeting concludes that a man scores above a questionnaire's cut-off, and the entry in his record states that he therefore 'has a moderate depressive episode'. Which criticism is correct?
questions.answer: A score above a cut-off is a measured finding that supports consideration of a category; the guideline's own account describes such thresholds as an indicator used to organise recommendations, so recording the score as the diagnosis inverts the relationship between measurement and judgement.
questions.distractor: The criticism is that questionnaire scores are meaningless in individual assessment, since the instruments were validated on groups and therefore nothing can be inferred about one person.
questions.correction: A group-validated instrument can still contribute useful evidence about an individual, and the guideline does recommend using a validated measure to inform and evaluate care; the error is not using it but treating it as the conclusion. The same instrument can perform very differently depending on the population and the prevalence, and a clinician who wants to reason about what a positive result means needs the base rates in the setting, not only the cut-off. So the repair is to record the score as a score, alongside the reported and observed material, and to let the formulation carry the position - marked as a position, with a review date.

questions.prompt: A fictional service considers using a screening questionnaire with a sensitivity of about 90 per cent and a specificity of about 90 per cent. In a first-contact population where roughly 1 in 100 people has the condition being screened for, what does the arithmetic imply about positive results?
questions.answer: About one in twelve positive results would be true positives: at a prevalence of one per cent, a test with those properties has a positive predictive value of about 8 per cent, so the great majority of positives would be false positives.
questions.distractor: About nine in ten positive results would be true positives, because a sensitivity of 90 per cent means that 90 per cent of positive results are correct.
questions.correction: Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the condition who test positive, not the proportion of positives who have the condition; the latter is the positive predictive value, and it depends on prevalence. Using an illustrative round cohort of 10,000 people at one per cent prevalence: 100 have the condition and 90 of them test positive, while 9,900 do not and 990 of them test positive, so 90 of 1,080 positives, about 8.3 per cent, are true positives. The same test at a prevalence of five per cent yields about 32 per cent, and in a population where 40 per cent have the condition, about 86 per cent. This is the arithmetic behind lesson 65's warning about screening in low-prevalence settings: it is a reason to use instruments where the prior probability is higher and to state the reasoning in the record rather than treating a positive result as a diagnosis.

questions.prompt: A fictional team is asked to introduce a stratified risk-category system after a serious incident, with every person given a low, medium or high label at the end of assessment. A senior clinician objects. Which objection is best supported by the guidance cited in this level?
questions.answer: The objection is that the guidance directs services not to use tools or scales to identify or stratify people by risk, because such instruments cannot predict repetition, and it asks instead for a written formulation of needs, of situations that would raise risk, and of planned actions, developed with the person.
questions.distractor: The objection is merely procedural: stratification is acceptable in principle, but the labels in the proposed system should be renamed from low, medium and high to something less stigmatising before it is introduced.
questions.correction: The guidance cited in lesson 66 goes to the substance rather than the vocabulary: it states that tools and scales, including those combining several risk factors, should not be used to predict suicide or repeat self-harm, that people should not be stratified into risk categories on the basis of such tools, and it directs that risk scales should not be used to determine the level of service a person receives. The reasoning given in the accompanying rationale concerns the properties of the instruments rather than the labels, and it also notes the implication of stability that categories create. The senior clinician's alternative is the formulation, and lesson 70 shows what that document consists of in writing.

questions.prompt: A fictional trainee reads that poor insight is associated with poorer treatment adherence and that good insight is associated with depression and lower self-reported quality of life, and concludes that the service should stop pushing people to recognise their difficulties. What is the error?
questions.answer: Both findings are correlational associations reported from samples defined by diagnosis, so they cannot license a change of practice in either direction; what they do support is recording which aspect of awareness is at issue and helping the person to integrate painful experience rather than to concede a label.
questions.distractor: The error is the opposite of what the trainee thinks: because insight predicts adherence, the service should treat recognition of illness as an outcome to be pursued regardless of the person's mood.
questions.correction: Neither reading is supported. The review cited in lesson 67 reports the two patterns in opposite directions in the same literature, which is precisely why it argues against treating insight as a single quantity to be increased, and its integrative model describes insight as requiring the integration of difficult information about internal states, circumstances, other people's perspectives and the person's life trajectory. The reported association with suicidality in some samples is correlational and concerns measured variables across groups, not a prediction about an individual, and it must not be used to justify keeping a person less informed. The defensible practice is specific: name the dimension, record what the person said, and treat disagreement about explanation as a disagreement rather than a symptom.

questions.prompt: A fictional service's leaflet states that people who fall below the assessment threshold 'do not have a mental health problem and should access self-help resources'. Using this level's material, what is the objection?
questions.answer: The leaflet turns a service's access rule into a claim about the person: the definition of a disorder rests on clinically significant disturbance usually associated with distress or impairment, and a threshold set to organise recommendations or allocate capacity cannot establish that a person is not suffering.
questions.distractor: The objection is that the leaflet is accurate but insensitive, and the wording should be changed to say that the person's problem is not serious enough to warrant help.
questions.correction: The rewording in the distractor keeps the error. The published definition of a disorder is about clinically significant disturbance and usually about distress or impairment, and the second sentence of that same source adds a broader category covering mental states associated with significant distress or impairment in functioning, which is the recognition that significant suffering exists outside the disorder categories. NICE's account of its own thresholds is explicit that scale thresholds were used as an indicator of severity to organise recommendations. The correct repair is to separate the two statements: this service can help at this severity; here is what it offers and where else to go. That is an access statement, which the service is entitled to make, instead of a claim about whether the person is unwell.

questions.prompt: A fictional 34-year-old man attends with low mood, poor sleep and irritability and reports drinking heavily most nights. The assessing clinician writes that the depression is primary and the drinking is a consequence, and arranges treatment for depression. Using this level's material, what is the main difficulty?
questions.answer: The direction of the relationship has been settled in a single appointment, when the guideline cited in lesson 69 expects comorbid mental health problems to be re-examined after a period of abstinence, typically three to four weeks, before they are treated as a separate problem - and the function of the drinking, which may be sleep, has not been assessed.
questions.distractor: The difficulty is that treatment for depression should never be arranged while a person is drinking, since no psychological or social intervention can work in the presence of alcohol use.
questions.correction: The distractor overstates the position and replaces one premature conclusion with another: the point is the sequencing of the assessment, not a prohibition, and the guideline's observation period exists because the clinical picture may clarify once use has stopped, which is a reason to keep the question open rather than to withhold everything. The assessment also lost the function question, so nothing in the record explains what the drinking is doing at night, and it lost the person's own goal. A better version records the reported pattern with quantities and timing, asks what the drinking does for him, notes prior attempts to stop and what happened, marks the direction of the relationship as undetermined, and states what would resolve it.

questions.prompt: A fictional assessment document is complete, well organised and accurate, but it lists only the areas that were covered in the appointment. Later readers cannot tell whether substance use, developmental history and current risk were asked about and denied, or never asked. Which repair follows from this level's material on documenting uncertainty?
questions.answer: Record the material that was not assessed as not assessed, alongside the negative findings that were examined, and record the decision to take no further action as a decision, with a review date - because a gap in the record and a negative finding look identical to the next reader.
questions.distractor: No repair is needed: a record should contain only the findings that were obtained, since documentation of what was not covered encourages a defensive style of practice and creates unnecessary exposure.
questions.correction: A record that distinguishes a negative finding from an absent inquiry is more useful and, in the record-keeping guidance cited in lesson 70, its content requirements point the same way: decisions made and actions agreed, including decisions to take no action, and when those decisions should be reviewed, are part of what the record should contain. A reader who cannot tell an unasked question from a denied one may repeat the appointment's work or, worse, assume that an area was cleared when it was never touched, which is the same error as reading silence as evidence that lesson 62 addresses. The practice is not defensive but operational: it tells the next clinician what to do first.

questions.prompt: A fictional team assesses a man who speaks little English and who has been described in his referral as 'vague and evasive'. The assessment is conducted with an interpreter over twenty-five minutes, and the trainee finds the material confusing. Which combination of this level's ideas is the best response?
questions.answer: Assess the direction of the interview, ask what level of English is adequate for the task at hand, brief the interpreter before the appointment and review the interpretation afterwards, slow the interview and keep the opening open rather than closed, and write down what remains unresolved instead of resolving it by inference.
questions.distractor: Replace the interpreter with a bilingual member of staff who knows the man socially, ask short closed questions because open questions are too difficult to interpret, and record the material as it stands so that no interpretation is added by the trainee.
questions.correction: Three of the distractor's elements are wrong, and each is answered by a specific lesson. An interpreter known to the person socially is the arrangement the guidance on interpreter use advises against, and the person should be offered a choice about the interpreter's characteristics. Closed questions make interpretation easier but produce the narrower and more discrepant material that lesson 62 warns about, and they are the wrong response to difficulty rather than a legitimate adaptation. And recording confusing material as if it were a finding is exactly the collapse of provenance that lesson 63 forbids; the note should say which questions the interpreter appears to have simplified, what was not covered, and that the record of the encounter is uncertain. The trainee's own account of the interview also belongs in the record, since familiarity with the person's use of language allows interpreters to render speech more accurately, as lesson 64 reports. The 'vague and evasive' description should not survive the appointment without evidence.

questions.prompt: A fictional 30-year-old woman declines an offered treatment. Her clinician records 'lacks insight into the need for treatment; not competent to decide'. Within the same week, the same woman gives a clear and consistent account of her finances, her housing and her reasons for refusing, and asks for a different treatment to be considered. Using this level's material, which statement is correct?
questions.answer: The record has merged two different tests: a judgement about awareness of illness was used to answer a legal question about decision-making capacity, and the specific evidence that would be needed for the capacity question - understanding, retaining, weighing and communicating the decision in question - was never recorded.
questions.distractor: The record is defensible, because a person who rejects a treatment that a clinician judges to be in her interests has by that fact shown that she cannot weigh information relevant to the decision.
questions.correction: That is the reasoning the lesson warns against in explicitly legal terms: disagreeing with a clinician is not the same as being unable to understand, retain, weigh or communicate a decision, and a decision made on the first basis while recording the language of the second is not defensible in a record whichever view one takes of the treatment. Note also what the same week's account shows: consistency over time and a coherent alternative request, which are exactly the kind of observations a capacity assessment rests on and which the first record did not contain. The repair is to separate the entries: one line on what she says about her difficulties, on the dimensions of insight that actually apply, and a separate, explicit statement about her decision-making about this treatment, with the evidence for whatever conclusion is drawn and a review date, which is the three-layer discipline of lesson 70 applied to a disagreement.
